GASTROINTESTINAL__Migratory Thrombophleb:
Migratory thrombophlebitis — Trousseau’s sign of malignancy — is recurrent superficial thrombophlebitis (tender, red, cord-like inflamed superficial veins) appearing in successive, changing sites.
  • Often in unusual places (arms, chest or trunk, not just varicose legs).
  • A paraneoplastic marker of an occult malignancy — classically pancreatic adenocarcinoma — driven by the hypercoagulable state of cancer.
  • Do not confuse it with Trousseau’s sign of latent tetany (carpal spasm on cuff inflation in hypocalcaemia) — a different sign with the same name.
🚨Migratory or recurrent unprovoked superficial thrombophlebitis — especially in unusual sites — is occult malignancy until proven otherwise: hunt for a cancer, above all pancreatic (see pancreatic cancer, Courvoisier’s sign). Assess for concurrent DVT / PE (see DVT / PE, swollen leg) — cancer-associated thrombosis can be life-threatening.

1Recognise & classify
🔍What it is
  • Superficial thrombophlebitis: a tender, red, cord-like palpable superficial vein
  • Migratory / recurrent: it resolves and reappears in different sites, often arms, chest or trunk
  • This migrating, multi-site pattern — not a single varicose-vein phlebitis — is what makes it Trousseau’s sign of malignancy
🚩When it matters
  • Occult malignancy until proven otherwise — investigate, above all for pancreatic cancer (see pancreatic cancer)
  • Assess for concurrent DVT / PE (cancer-associated thrombosis) (see DVT / PE)
  • Do not confuse with Trousseau’s sign of latent tetany (carpal spasm, hypocalcaemia) — same name, different sign
🟠Malignant associations
  • Pancreatic adenocarcinoma — the classic and strongest association (see pancreatic cancer, jaundice)
  • Other adenocarcinomas: lung (see lung cancer), gastric (see gastric cancer), colorectal (see colorectal cancer) and ovarian
  • Look for other cancer clues: weight loss, jaundice, new diabetes (pancreatic)
🧬Mechanism (why it happens)
  • A cancer-associated hypercoagulable state — tumours release tissue factor and mucins that activate coagulation
  • Result: recurrent venous thromboses (superficial and deep) — part of the spectrum of cancer-associated thrombosis
  • The same procoagulant drive underlies the raised VTE risk in malignancy
🔬Distinguish
  • Ordinary superficial thrombophlebitis: single site, often a varicose vein or cannula — not migratory, not paraneoplastic
  • DVT: deep, whole-limb swelling — may coexist with or follow the superficial phlebitis (see DVT / PE)
  • The two Trousseau’s signs: malignancy (migratory phlebitis) vs latent tetany (carpal spasm, hypocalcaemia)
🩺Assess, investigate & manage
  • Examine the phlebitic cords and take a cancer history (weight loss, jaundice, GI / respiratory symptoms)
  • Investigate for occult cancer: bloods, CT chest / abdomen / pelvis, age-appropriate screen, tumour markers (e.g. CA 19-9); Doppler US for DVT
  • Treat the underlying cancer; anticoagulate cancer-associated VTE with LMWH or a DOAC (LMWH preferred in luminal GI / genitourinary tumours; warfarin is relatively ineffective here — see anticoagulation)

GASTROINTESTINAL__Courvoisier's Sign:
Courvoisier’s sign is a palpable, non-tender (enlarged) gallbladder in a patient with painless jaundice.
  • Courvoisier’s law: in this setting the cause is unlikely to be gallstones — chronic stone disease fibroses and shrinks the gallbladder so it cannot distend.
  • A distended, palpable gallbladder therefore implies a different, distal bile-duct obstruction — usually a malignancy (carcinoma of the head of the pancreas, cholangiocarcinoma or an ampullary tumour).
  • The headline: painless obstructive jaundice is cancer until proven otherwise.
🚨Painless obstructive jaundice with a palpable gallbladder = malignancy until proven otherwise — most often pancreatic head cancer (see pancreatic cancer, jaundice). Refer urgently on a suspected-cancer (2-week-wait) pathway. If the patient is febrile with rigors, treat concurrent ascending cholangitis (see ascending cholangitis). Do not be reassured by the absence of pain.

1Recognise & classify
🔍What it is & the law
  • Palpable, non-tender gallbladder + painless jaundice = Courvoisier’s sign
  • Courvoisier’s law: this is unlikely to be gallstones — chronic stones fibrose / shrink the gallbladder so it cannot distend
  • So the obstruction is distal (CBD) and usually malignant, causing back-pressure and gallbladder distension
🚩When it matters
  • Painless obstructive jaundice = malignancy until proven otherwise — urgent 2-week-wait referral (see pancreatic cancer)
  • Look for weight loss, anorexia, dark urine, pale stools, pruritus and (late) epigastric / back pain
  • Fever / rigors → concurrent ascending cholangitis — a biliary-sepsis emergency (see cholangitis)
🟠Malignant causes
  • Carcinoma of the head of the pancreas — the classic cause of painless obstructive jaundice (see pancreatic cancer)
  • Cholangiocarcinoma of the distal common bile duct (see cholangiocarcinoma)
  • Ampullary carcinoma (may give intermittent jaundice + GI bleeding / silver stools) and, less often, duodenal tumours
🪨The gallstone caveat
  • The “law” is a rule of thumb, not absolute — a CBD stone can rarely cause it if the gallbladder never became fibrosed
  • A cystic-duct stone can cause a mucocele / hydrops (palpable, often non-tender, but with no jaundice as the CBD is patent); Mirizzi (a stone compressing the common hepatic duct) can jaundice but is a proximal, benign cause
  • The teaching point still holds: do not assume gallstones (see gallstone disease)
🔬Distinguish & associated signs
  • vs acute cholecystitis: that gallbladder is palpable but tender with a positive Murphy’s (see Murphy’s sign) and jaundice is usually absent
  • Look for a hard epigastric mass (see abdominal mass), new-onset diabetes and migratory thrombophlebitis (Trousseau’s sign of malignancy)
  • Obstructive (post-hepatic) jaundice pattern: dark urine, pale stools, pruritus (see jaundice)
🩺Assess & investigate
  • LFTs: obstructive pattern (raised ALP / GGT, conjugated bilirubin); CA 19-9 tumour marker
  • Ultrasound first (dilated CBD, distended gallbladder, pancreatic mass); then CT pancreas (staging), MRCP and EUS + biopsy
  • Manage the cause: ERCP stent for relief of jaundice; Whipple’s (pancreaticoduodenectomy) if resectable

Think malignant distal CBD obstruction — pancreatic head cancer first. Painless obstructive jaundice is cancer until proven otherwise.

GASTROINTESTINAL__Grey Turner's & Cullen:
Cullen’s sign (periumbilical bruising) and Grey Turner’s sign (flank bruising) are ecchymoses — blood from a retroperitoneal or intra-abdominal haemorrhage tracking along fascial planes to the skin.
  • They are delayed (appearing over 24–48 h), insensitive and non-specific — so their absence never reassures.
  • Classically taught with severe acute (necrotising) pancreatitis, where they mark a poor prognosis.
  • But the real message is a significant bleed — think ruptured AAA and ruptured ectopic too.
🚨These bruises signal significant intra-abdominal / retroperitoneal bleeding — assess for shock and start ABCDE + major-haemorrhage resuscitation. Exclude the killers: a ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm (back / flank pain, pulsatile mass, collapse — see AAA) and, in any woman of childbearing age, a ruptured ectopic pregnancy (β-hCG — see ectopic). In pancreatitis they mark severe / necrotising disease.

1Recognise & classify
🔍What they are
  • Cullen’s sign: periumbilical bruising / bluish discolouration around the umbilicus
  • Grey Turner’s sign: flank bruising along the loins
  • Blood from a retroperitoneal / intra-abdominal bleed tracks to the skin — delayed 24–48 h, so early absence does not exclude a bleed
🚩When it matters
  • They mean a significant bleed → look for shock; ABCDE + major-haemorrhage protocol
  • Exclude the killers: ruptured AAA (see AAA, pulsatile mass) and ruptured ectopic (β-hCG, see ectopic)
  • In acute pancreatitis they signal severe / necrotising disease and a worse prognosis
🟠Severe acute pancreatitis (the classic)
  • Haemorrhagic / necrotising pancreatitis — retroperitoneal bleeding tracks to the skin (see acute pancreatitis)
  • Uncommon (present in a small minority) but a marker of severity — score with Glasgow / APACHE II
  • Look for the pancreatitis picture: epigastric pain to the back, vomiting, raised amylase / lipase
🩸Vascular & haemorrhage causes
  • Ruptured AAA — retroperitoneal bleed; the must-exclude vascular killer (see abdominal aortic aneurysm)
  • Ruptured ectopic pregnancy — intraperitoneal blood (see early pregnancy complications)
  • Splenic / hepatic rupture and blunt abdominal trauma; a bleeding ruptured ovarian cyst
💊Coagulopathy & other
  • Anticoagulation / bleeding disorders — a spontaneous retroperitoneal or rectus-sheath bleed (see anticoagulation)
  • DIC and other coagulopathies (see DIC)
  • Ruptured visceral artery aneurysm (e.g. splenic) and spontaneous retroperitoneal haemorrhage
🩺Assess & investigate
  • ABCDE, vital signs and signs of shock; palpate for a pulsatile mass (see abdominal pain, acute abdomen)
  • Bloods: FBC, clotting, group & save / crossmatch, amylase / lipase, U&E, β-hCG (women)
  • CT abdomen / pelvis with contrast to locate the bleed (or bedside FAST / USS in trauma / instability)
Cullen’s = umbilicus, Grey Turner’s = flank — both are late, insensitive skin markers of a retroperitoneal / intra-abdominal bleed. They are classic for severe pancreatitis but the priority is to resuscitate and exclude a ruptured AAA or ectopic. Never wait for them to appear.

GASTROINTESTINAL__Rovsing's Sign:
Rovsing’s sign is positive when pressing on the LEFT iliac fossa (LLQ) provokes pain in the RIGHT iliac fossa (RLQ) — localised peritoneal irritation over the appendix, so it points to acute appendicitis.
  • It sits within the appendicitis sign cluster — McBurney’s-point tenderness, the psoas and obturator signs, and rebound tenderness.
  • But RIF pain has a broad differential, and the sign is neither very sensitive nor specific.
  • In any woman of childbearing age, exclude an ectopic pregnancy first.
🚨In any woman of childbearing age with RIF pain, do a β-hCG to exclude an ectopic pregnancy — it can cause fatal haemorrhage (see early pregnancy complications). Watch for generalised peritonitis from a perforated appendix (rigid, still abdomen — see peritonism). Remember atypical presentations in the very young, elderly and pregnant (the appendix rises in pregnancy), where signs are misleading.

1Recognise & classify
🔍What it is & how to elicit
  • Press deeply and steadily in the LEFT iliac fossa — positive if the patient feels pain in the RIGHT iliac fossa
  • Reflects localised peritoneal irritation over the appendix; the gentle equivalents are percussion / cough tenderness and, in children, the hop test (RIF pain on hopping)
  • It is a supportive, not diagnostic, sign — low sensitivity and specificity; use it with the whole picture
🚩When it matters
  • Woman of childbearing age? → β-hCG to exclude an ectopic pregnancy before anything else (see ectopic / early pregnancy)
  • Rigid, board-like, still abdomen → generalised peritonitis from a perforated appendix (see peritonism, acute abdomen)
  • Very young / elderly / pregnant present atypically — a normal-looking exam does not exclude it
🟠Acute appendicitis (the positive)
  • Luminal obstruction (faecolith / lymphoid hyperplasia) → central colicky pain migrating to the RIF over 12–24 h, anorexia, nausea, low-grade fever (see acute appendicitis)
  • The sign cluster: McBurney’s tenderness, Rovsing’s, rebound / guarding, psoas (retrocaecal) and obturator (pelvic) signs
  • Raised WCC / CRP; use the Alvarado score to support the clinical diagnosis
♀️Gynaecological mimics
  • Ectopic pregnancy — positive β-hCG, PV bleeding, shock; the must-exclude diagnosis
  • Ovarian torsion (sudden severe pain, adnexal mass — see ovarian torsion) and a ruptured / haemorrhagic ovarian cyst
  • PID / tubo-ovarian abscess (discharge, cervical excitation — see pelvic infection) and mittelschmerz
🌀Other mimics
  • Mesenteric adenitis (children, post-viral, higher fever, less localised) and a Meckel’s diverticulitis
  • Terminal ileitis / Crohn’s (see IBD), caecal diverticulitis and caecal cancer in the elderly (see diverticular disease)
  • Right UTI / renal colic, and (rarely) referred testicular torsion — check the urine and the scrotum
🩺Assess & investigate
  • Full abdominal exam (see abdominal pain); check psoas / obturator signs and for peritonism
  • Bloods: FBC, CRP; urine dip + β-hCG (women); the Alvarado score stratifies risk
  • Imaging: USS first (esp. children / women — also assesses ovaries), CT abdomen where diagnosis is unclear (esp. elderly)

GASTROINTESTINAL__Murphy's Sign:
Murphy’s sign is a bedside test for acute cholecystitis.
  • Technique: place your fingers at the right upper quadrant (costal margin, mid-clavicular line, over the gallbladder fundus) and ask the patient to breathe in deeply.
  • A positive sign: as the diaphragm pushes the inflamed gallbladder onto your hand, the patient catches their breath and stops (arrest of inspiration) from pain.
  • It is only valid if the same manoeuvre on the LEFT is negative.
  • Use it to anchor the patient in the biliary spectrum — biliary colic, cholecystitis, cholangitis and common-bile-duct stones.
🚨Charcot’s triad — RUQ pain + fever / rigors + jaundice — is ascending cholangitis, a life-threatening biliary sepsis needing urgent antibiotics and biliary decompression (ERCP) (see ascending cholangitis, jaundice); add hypotension + confusion for Reynolds’ pentad. Beware the complications of cholecystitis (empyema, gangrene, perforation) and acalculous cholecystitis in the critically ill (sepsis, trauma, TPN), where signs are blunted.

  • Constant RUQ pain >6 h, fever, positive Murphy’s, raised WCC / CRP (see acute cholecystitis)

  • LFTs often near-normal — markedly deranged / jaundiced suggests a CBD stone or Mirizzi

  • Choledocholithiasis: CBD stone → obstructive jaundice, dilated CBD, deranged LFTs
  • Gallstone pancreatitis: epigastric pain to the back, raised amylase / lipase (see acute pancreatitis)
🌀Mimics / false positives
  • Acute hepatitis — tender RUQ, deranged LFTs (see acute hepatitis)
  • Right lower-lobe pneumonia and right pleurisy can irritate the RUQ
  • Fitz-Hugh–Curtis (perihepatitis in PID) and a retrocaecal appendix — Murphy’s is not perfectly specific (false positives occur)

  • Check for jaundice and fever; examine the RUQ (see abdominal pain, acute abdomen)
  • Bloods: FBC, CRP, LFTs, amylase / lipase, blood cultures if septic
  • First-line imaging = ultrasound (stones, wall >3 mm, pericholecystic fluid, sonographic Murphy’s); MRCP for CBD stones

GASTROINTESTINAL__Dupuytren's Contractur:
Dupuytren’s contracture is a fibroproliferative disease of the palmar fascia.
  • It progresses from a painless palmar nodule (classically at the base of the ring finger) to a palpable cord and finally a fixed flexion contracture of the ring and little fingers (MCP then PIP joints).
  • A recognised stigma of chronic liver disease, but the great majority are idiopathic / hereditary (autosomal-dominant, Northern-European ‘Viking’ descent) — so do not assume alcohol.
  • Screen the cross-system associations and assess function with the Hueston tabletop test.
🚨Dupuytren’s is chronic, not an emergency — the pitfalls are diagnostic. It is a disease of the palmar fascia (a palpable cord with secondary skin tethering and a passive contracture), not a tendon or nerve problem — distinguish it from trigger finger (catching tendon nodule), ulnar claw (neurological) and tendon injury. Spot the aggressive Dupuytren’s diathesis (young, bilateral, strong family history, ectopic disease) and refer when the tabletop test is positive or function is impaired.

GASTROINTESTINAL__Asterixis (Liver Flap):
Asterixis (the “flapping tremor” or liver flap) is a negative myoclonus — brief, irregular lapses of posture, not a true tremor.
  • Elicit it: ask the patient to hold both arms out, dorsiflex the wrists (“stop the traffic”) and spread the fingers, then watch for 30 seconds — the hands flap as tone is momentarily lost.
  • It is a sign of metabolic encephalopathy from any cause — not just the liver.
  • The single most useful split: bilateral (metabolic — hepatic, CO₂ retention, uraemia, drugs) vs unilateral (a contralateral structural brain lesion).
🚨Asterixis + drowsiness / confusion = decompensated encephalopathy — act on it. In chronic liver disease think hepatic encephalopathy and hunt the precipitant (GI bleed, infection / SBP, constipation, sedatives, electrolyte upset, dehydration, high protein load). In known COPD, a flap with drowsiness signals CO₂ narcosis — do an ABG and give controlled oxygen, never uncontrolled high-flow. A unilateral flap is a structural stroke until proven otherwise — image the brain.

GASTROINTESTINAL__Leukonychia:
Leukonychia is whitening of the nails. First split it:
  • True leukonychia — the nail plate itself is white; it moves distally with growth and does not blanch on pressure.
  • Apparent leukonychia — the nail bed is pale; it blanches and does not move with growth.
  • The named patterns — diffuse true whitening (leukonychia totalis), Terry’s nails and Muehrcke’s lines — are markers of hypoalbuminaemia from any cause (cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome, protein-losing enteropathy, malnutrition), not just liver disease.
  • Recognise the named patterns and find the low-albumin cause.
🚨Diffuse leukonychia / Terry’s nails / Muehrcke’s lines point to hypoalbuminaemia — look for its cause across systems: chronic liver disease (see cirrhosis, ascites, jaundice), nephrotic syndrome, protein-losing enteropathy and malnutrition. Mees’ lines (transverse white bands that grow out) suggest arsenic / heavy-metal poisoning or chemotherapy — a different, toxic differential.

GASTROINTESTINAL__Caput Medusae:
Caput medusae is a cluster of dilated, tortuous veins radiating from the umbilicus, from recanalisation of the umbilical / paraumbilical veins (in the falciform ligament) — a sign of portal hypertension, not an oestrogen effect.
  • The mechanism: blood is shunted from the high-pressure portal system to the systemic veins of the abdominal wall.
  • The key bedside step — the direction-of-flow test: in portal hypertension flow radiates away from the umbilicus, whereas in IVC obstruction the veins below the umbilicus flow upwards.
  • Look for the company it keeps — ascites, splenomegaly and varices.
🚨Caput medusae means portal hypertension — so the patient is at risk of oesophageal / gastric varices and variceal bleeding (see Vomiting Blood & Black Stools); arrange endoscopic screening and manage the liver disease. Distinguish it from inferior vena cava obstruction (abdominal-wall collaterals with upward flow below the umbilicus) — a different cause and work-up.

🔍Recognise it
  • Dilated, tortuous veins radiating out from the umbilicus across the abdominal wall
  • A sign of portal hypertension — look for the company it keeps: ascites, splenomegaly, and other stigmata (see spider naevi)
  • A venous hum may be audible at the umbilicus (Cruveilhier-Baumgarten murmur)
🚩Why it matters
  • It signals portal hypertension → oesophageal / gastric varices and a risk of variceal bleeding (see haematemesis & melaena)
  • Arrange endoscopic variceal screening and manage the underlying liver disease
  • Do not mistake it for IVC obstruction — a different cause with different management
🧭Direction-of-flow test
  • Empty a vein below the umbilicus with two fingers, release one, and watch which way it refills
  • Portal hypertension (caput medusae): flow radiates away from the umbilicus (downward below it — the normal direction)
  • IVC obstruction: flow below the umbilicus is upward (reversed), diverting blood past the blocked IVC
🫀Mechanism
  • Portal hypertension reopens the umbilical vein via paraumbilical veins (in the falciform ligament) connecting to the left portal vein
  • Blood is shunted to the systemic epigastric / abdominal-wall veins around the umbilicus
  • A patent shunt can produce the Cruveilhier-Baumgarten hum (a venous murmur at the umbilicus)
🧬Causes (portal hypertension)
  • Hepatic (commonest): cirrhosis of any cause (see cirrhosis / alcohol)
  • Pre-hepatic: portal vein thrombosis (splenomegaly with a normal liver)
  • Post-hepatic: Budd-Chiari syndrome / right heart failure

GASTROINTESTINAL__Palmar Erythema:
Palmar erythema is symmetrical redness of the palms — over the thenar and hypothenar eminences (and finger pulps), classically sparing the central palm; it is warm and blanches on pressure.
  • Like spider naevi, it reflects relative oestrogen excess and can be physiological (familial, pregnancy) or a marker of systemic disease.
  • Work the cross-system differential: chronic liver disease, high-oestrogen states, thyrotoxicosis, rheumatoid arthritis, polycythaemia — or a normal variant.
  • It is a soft sign: interpret it in the company it keeps.
🚨Palmar erythema is not dangerous in itself but is a clue to systemic disease. With spider naevi and other stigmata it points to chronic liver disease (check LFTs and look for jaundice and ascites). Do not over-call an isolated, lifelong, familial finding — but a new, symmetrical erythema warrants a search for liver, thyroid, rheumatological or haematological disease.

GASTROINTESTINAL__Spider Naevi:
A spider naevus is a central dilated arteriole with radiating ‘legs’ (telangiectasia) that blanches on central pressure and refills from the centre outwards — found in the distribution of the superior vena cava (face, neck, upper chest and arms).
  • It reflects relative excess oestrogen.
  • Number matters: up to five small naevi can be normal, but more than five (or a new crop) is pathological — most importantly chronic liver disease.
  • Work the cross-system differential (liver, high-oestrogen states, thyrotoxicosis, normal) and distinguish the mimics.
🚨More than five spider naevi, or a new crop, is a sign of chronic liver disease until proven otherwise — look for the other stigmata (palmar erythema, gynaecomastia, jaundice, ascites) and check LFTs. Do not confuse them with hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia (mucosal lesions + epistaxis, do not blanch from a central point) or SVC obstruction (fixed, dilated, non-blanching veins with facial oedema).

GASTROINTESTINAL__Hepatomegaly & Splenom:
Hepatomegaly (an enlarged liver, RUQ) and splenomegaly (an enlarged spleen, LUQ) are organomegaly found on palpation.
  • First decide which organ: both move with respiration, are dull to percussion and you cannot get above them.
  • But the spleen has a notch, enlarges towards the RIF, and is not ballotable — whereas a kidney is ballotable / bimanual with a band of resonance over it.
  • Then work the cause: hepatomegaly, splenomegaly (including the massive shortlist), or both (hepatosplenomegaly).
  • Look for ascites (see Ascites) and jaundice.
🚨A hard, craggy, irregular liver (± weight loss) is metastases or hepatocellular carcinoma until proven otherwise. Splenomegaly + lymphadenopathy, B symptoms or abnormal blood counts points to a haematological malignancy (leukaemia / lymphoma). Warn patients with splenomegaly to avoid contact sports (risk of splenic rupture), and think of it after trauma or in glandular fever.

GASTROINTESTINAL__Ascites:
Ascites is free fluid in the peritoneal cavity — presenting as abdominal swelling, weight gain and an everted umbilicus (one of the ‘six F’s’ of abdominal distension).
  • Confirm it: shifting dullness, a fluid thrill, ultrasound.
  • Split the cause with the SAAG (serum-ascites albumin gradient): ≥11 g/L = portal hypertension (cirrhosis, heart failure); <11 = a non-portal cause (malignancy, TB, pancreatitis, nephrotic).
  • Always tap new ascites — for SAAG, a neutrophil count (SBP), cytology and culture.
  • Then screen the red flags: SBP, tense ascites, malignancy.
🚨In a patient with known ascites, fever, abdominal pain, or new encephalopathy / deterioration is spontaneous bacterial peritonitis until a diagnostic tap excludes it — an ascitic neutrophil count ≥250 cells/mm³ confirms it (treat with cefotaxime + IV albumin, which reduces hepatorenal syndrome). New ascites with weight loss → suspect malignancy (send cytology). Tense ascites with breathlessness needs therapeutic paracentesis.

GASTROINTESTINAL__Jaundice:
Jaundice is yellow discolouration of the sclera and skin from a raised bilirubin (clinically visible above ~50 µmol/L).
  • Split it three ways: pre-hepatic (unconjugated — haemolysis, Gilbert’s), hepatic (hepatocellular — hepatitis, alcohol, drugs, cirrhosis) and post-hepatic (conjugated / obstructive — stones, tumour, PBC / PSC).
  • Three clues localise it: urine (dark → conjugated), stool (pale → obstruction), itch (cholestasis).
  • Plus the LFT pattern: ↑ALT / AST = hepatocellular; ↑ALP / GGT = cholestatic.
  • Then screen the red flags: cholangitis, acute liver failure, painless malignant obstruction.
🚨Fever + right-upper-quadrant pain + jaundice (Charcot’s triad) is ascending cholangitis — a biliary-sepsis emergency needing antibiotics and urgent biliary drainage (ERCP); add confusion and shock and it is Reynolds’ pentad. Jaundice with encephalopathy and coagulopathy is acute liver failure (think paracetamol — give NAC). Painless jaundice with a palpable gallbladder (Courvoisier’s law) is pancreatic / biliary cancer until proven otherwise.

GASTROINTESTINAL__Groin Lump:
A groin lump is worked up by two questions: is it a hernia? and where is it relative to the pubic tubercle?
  • An inguinal hernia lies above and medial to the pubic tubercle; a femoral hernia lies below and lateral to it.
  • Read the character: a cough impulse and reducibility (hernia), pulsatile & expansile (femoral artery aneurysm), disappears on lying with a thrill (saphena varix), or it transilluminates (fluid).
  • The red flag: a tender, irreducible lump with no cough impulse is a strangulated hernia.
🚨A tender, irreducible groin lump with no cough impulse — especially with pain, vomiting or bowel obstruction — is a strangulated hernia (a surgical emergency: resuscitate, nil by mouth, urgent repair). Femoral hernias (commoner in women) have a high risk of strangulation and should be repaired promptly. Do not mistake a pulsatile, expansile lump (a femoral artery aneurysm) for a hernia.

GASTROINTESTINAL__Abdominal Distension:
Abdominal distension is a generalised swelling of the abdomen, classically worked through the six F’s:
  • Fat (obesity).
  • Fluid (ascites).
  • Flatus (gas — obstruction / ileus).
  • Faeces (constipation).
  • Fetus (pregnancy).
  • A big organ or mass (organomegaly, tumour, a distended bladder; see Abdominal Mass).
  • The examination pattern tells them apart: shifting dullness / a fluid thrill → fluid; resonant / tympanic → gas; you can’t get below it → pregnancy / bladder / pelvic. Then screen the red flags (obstruction, SBP, malignant ascites, perforation).
🚨Distension with colicky pain, vomiting and absolute constipation (no flatus) is bowel obstruction — make the patient nil by mouth, pass an NG tube and give IV fluids (“drip and suck”) and get surgical review. In known ascites, fever, abdominal pain or encephalopathy is spontaneous bacterial peritonitis until a tap excludes it. New ascites with weight loss → suspect malignancy; distension with peritonism / rigidity → a perforation.

GASTROINTESTINAL__Abdominal Mass:
An abdominal mass is worked up by two questions: where is it? (localise to one of the nine regions) and what is its character?
  • The classic bedside questions: is it pulsatile & expansile (an aneurysm; see Pulsatile Abdominal Mass)? Does it move with respiration (liver, spleen, kidney)? Is it ballotable (renal)?
  • Can you get above it? (no → an upper-abdominal organ, e.g. liver / spleen). Can you get below it? (no → it arises from the pelvis).
  • Add consistency (hard / craggy → malignant) and tenderness.
  • Region + character localises the organ; then screen the red flags (aneurysm, malignancy, sepsis).
🚨A central, pulsatile and expansile mass is an abdominal aortic aneurysm — if there is pain, tenderness or shock, treat as a rupture (urgent vascular review; do not delay for imaging in the unstable patient). A hard, craggy, fixed mass with weight loss or a hard left supraclavicular (Virchow’s) node is malignancy until proven otherwise. An acutely tender mass with fever / sepsis suggests an abscess, an appendix / diverticular phlegmon or obstruction.

GASTROINTESTINAL__Rectal Pain / Perianal:
Rectal / anal pain and a perianal lump are common anorectal presentations read at the bedside.
  • Characterise the pain: severe tearing pain on defecation → fissure; constant throbbing pain with a hot swelling and fever → abscess; a sudden, acutely painful lump → a thrombosed external pile.
  • Characterise the lump: position (clock-face), whether it is tender, reducible or discharging.
  • Split the acutely painful trio (abscess, thrombosed pile, fissure) from chronic lumps (prolapsing haemorrhoids, tags, fistula, prolapse).
  • Never miss perianal sepsis or an anal / rectal cancer. (For bleeding, see PR Bleeding.)
🚨A perianal abscess needs urgent surgical drainage (examination under anaesthesia) — antibiotics alone are not enough. In a diabetic or immunocompromised patient with pain out of proportion, crepitus, necrosis or systemic sepsis, think Fournier’s gangrene (necrotising fasciitis of the perineum — a surgical emergency: resuscitate, broad-spectrum antibiotics and immediate debridement). A hard, irregular, non-healing anal / rectal mass or ulcer with inguinal nodes (HPV / HIV risk) is anal / rectal cancer until proven otherwise — biopsy and refer on the suspected-cancer pathway.

GASTROINTESTINAL__PR Bleeding:
PR (rectal) bleeding is blood passed per rectum — usually a lower-GI source (distal to the ligament of Treitz), in contrast to melaena (black, tarry — an upper-GI bleed; see Vomiting Blood & Black Stools).
  • Colour: bright red = anorectal / distal; darker / plum = more proximal colon; maroon or brisk = a right-colon or a rapid upper bleed.
  • Relation to stool: on the paper / coating the stool = outlet; mixed through the stool = colonic.
  • Then work the differential by pattern, screen the red flags (colorectal cancer), and resuscitate the acute severe bleed.
🚨Do not blame haemorrhoids for rectal bleeding in an older patient without excluding colorectal cancer (change in bowel habit, weight loss, iron-deficiency anaemia, a mass, or age ≥50 with rectal bleeding → suspected-cancer pathway; see Change in Bowel Habit). Large-volume PR bleeding with shock → resuscitate (ABCDE, crossmatch, major haemorrhage protocol). And remember a brisk upper-GI bleed can present as red PR blood — do an OGD if unstable with no lower source. In anyone with a previous aortic-graft repair, a small ‘herald’ bleed then massive haemorrhage is an aorto-enteric fistula until proven otherwise.

GASTROINTESTINAL__Steatorrhoea:
Steatorrhoea is pale, bulky, greasy, foul-smelling stool that floats and is hard to flush — the hallmark of fat malabsorption.
  • Digesting fat needs three things: pancreatic lipase, bile (to emulsify it) and a healthy small-bowel mucosa (to absorb it).
  • So it localises to three buckets: pancreatic exocrine insufficiency, bile deficiency / cholestasis, or small-bowel / mucosal disease.
  • Look for weight loss and fat-soluble vitamin (A, D, E, K) deficiency.
  • Work it in three moves: recognise it, localise the mechanism, and investigate (faecal elastase, coeliac serology, imaging). See also Diarrhoea.
🚨Do not miss pancreatic cancer — steatorrhoea with painless obstructive jaundice and weight loss (it blocks both the pancreatic duct and the bile duct; see Jaundice). Watch for fat-soluble vitamin deficiency: vitamin K → bleeding / raised INR, vitamin D → osteomalacia / hypocalcaemia, vitamin A → night blindness, vitamin E → neurological signs. New steatorrhoea with weight loss in an older patient needs prompt investigation.

Constipation is infrequent (<3 stools/week) or difficult defecation — hard or lumpy stool, straining, a sense of incomplete evacuation or blockage, and needing manual manoeuvres.

  • Work it in three moves: characterise, exclude secondary causes, and manage (lifestyle → the laxative ladder), treating any impaction. (See also Change in Bowel Habit.)
🚨Red flags: new constipation ≥60, PR bleeding, weight loss, iron-deficiency anaemia or an abdominal / rectal mass → suspect colorectal cancer.   • Colorectal cancer / stricture, bowel obstruction, diverticular stricture

GASTROINTESTINAL__Diarrhoea:
Diarrhoea is the passage of ≥3 loose or watery stools a day (or a persistent increase in looseness / frequency; >200 g/day). Two axes solve it.
  • Duration: acute (<2 weeks — usually infective and self-limiting) vs chronic (>4 weeks — needs a work-up, as for a change in bowel habit).
  • For chronic disease, the mechanism — secretory, osmotic, inflammatory or malabsorptive.
  • The core skills: assessing dehydration & red flags, and knowing when (and when NOT) to investigate or give antibiotics — most acute diarrhoea is viral and needs only rehydration.
🚨Red flags: blood in the stool (dysentery, IBD, ischaemia), dehydration / shock / sepsis, recent antibiotics or hospital stay (C. difficile), immunocompromise, and severe pain with a distended abdomen (toxic megacolon). Chronic features (weight loss, nocturnal diarrhoea, >4–6 weeks) need investigation. Do not give loperamide or antibiotics in suspected E. coli O157 (haemolytic-uraemic syndrome risk) or C. difficile.

GASTROINTESTINAL__Change in Bowel Habit:
A change in bowel habit is a persistent change in the frequency, consistency or form of the stool — new looser / more frequent motions, or new constipation. It can be the first sign of colorectal cancer.
  • Characterise the change: what, how long, blood, weight loss.
  • Screen the red flags that trigger the suspected-cancer pathway (FIT & colonoscopy).
  • Work the differential: structural (cancer, IBD, diverticular), functional / malabsorptive (IBS, coeliac) and systemic / drug causes.
  • For symptom-specific detail see Diarrhoea and Constipation.
🚨Screen for colorectal cancer: a persistent change to looser / more frequent stool (especially ≥60), rectal bleeding (see PR Bleeding), iron-deficiency anaemia, unexplained weight loss, or an abdominal / rectal mass → the suspected-cancer (2-week-wait) pathway, guided by a FIT test. Do not label a first presentation as IBS in an older patient or anyone with red flags. Also consider C. difficile after antibiotics and new inflammatory bowel disease. And remember a negative FIT does not exclude cancer — still refer with a mass, unexplained iron-deficiency anaemia or persistent concern.

🔍Characterise the change
  • What changed: frequency, consistency (Bristol stool chart), and form (new pencil-thin or pellety stool)

  • Colorectal cancer — the must-exclude in a new, persistent change

  • Irritable bowel syndrome — pain relieved by defecation, bloating, altered habit; a diagnosis of exclusion with no red flags

GASTROINTESTINAL__Vomiting Blood & Black:
Vomiting blood (haematemesis — fresh red if brisk, or ‘coffee-ground’ once altered by stomach acid) and black, tarry stools (melaena — digested blood, black, sticky and offensive) are the cardinal signs of an upper-GI bleed (proximal to the ligament of Treitz).
  • Fresh red blood per rectum instead points to a lower-GI source (see PR Bleeding).
  • It is a medical emergency: resuscitate first.
  • Then risk-score: Glasgow-Blatchford before endoscopy, Rockall after.
  • Treat by cause — the decisive split is variceal vs non-variceal.
🚨Treat a significant bleed as a haemorrhage emergency: shock (tachycardia, hypotension, oliguria), ongoing haematemesis, or a large-volume bleed → ABCDE, two large-bore cannulae, crossmatch and the major haemorrhage protocol. A normal early haemoglobin does not exclude a big bleed (haemodilution lags). In known / suspected liver disease, assume varices and give terlipressin + antibiotics at once.

1Recognise & resuscitate
🔍Recognise & define
  • Haematemesis: vomiting fresh red blood (brisk) or ‘coffee-ground’ vomit (altered by acid)
  • Melaena: black, tarry, sticky, offensive stool — digested blood from an upper-GI source
  • Distinguish from haemoptysis (coughed, frothy, bright) and fresh red PR bleeding (a lower-GI source)

  • ABCDE; two large-bore cannulae; FBC, U&E, LFTs, clotting, group & crossmatch; fluids / blood
  • Major haemorrhage protocol if massive; correct coagulopathy (reverse anticoagulants; platelets / FFP as needed); catheter; NBM
  • Restrictive transfusion (target Hb ~70–90 g/L) unless massive / unstable — a normal early Hb can mislead
🩸Non-variceal causes
  • Peptic ulcer disease — the commonest cause (H. pylori, NSAIDs)
  • Gastritis / erosions, oesophagitis, and a Mallory-Weiss tear (after a retching / vomiting bout)
  • Malignancy (gastric / oesophageal), and rarer Dieulafoy lesion / angiodysplasia
🫀Variceal cause — the critical split
  • Oesophageal / gastric varices from portal hypertension (usually cirrhosis / alcohol)
  • Suspect with known liver disease, alcohol excess, or stigmata of chronic liver disease
  • High mortality — give terlipressin + prophylactic antibiotics and arrange band ligation
🧾Risk scoring & the urea clue
  • Glasgow-Blatchford (pre-endoscopy): uses urea, Hb, BP, pulse, melaena, syncope, liver / cardiac disease — a score of 0 (some units use ≤1) may allow outpatient management
  • Rockall (post-endoscopy): age, shock, comorbidity, diagnosis & endoscopic stigmata → rebleeding / mortality risk

  • Endoscopy (OGD) within 24 h (sooner after resuscitation if unstable) — diagnostic and therapeutic
  • Non-variceal: endoscopic haemostasis (adrenaline injection plus a clip / thermal method) then high-dose IV PPI
  • Variceal: terlipressin + antibiotics then band ligation; rescue with balloon tamponade → TIPS

GASTROINTESTINAL__Painful Swallowing (Od:
Painful swallowing (odynophagia) is pain on swallowing — distinct from difficulty swallowing (dysphagia), though the two often coexist.
  • It points strongly to inflammation or ulceration of the swallowing tract.
  • Localise: oropharyngeal (a sore throat, pain at the start of the swallow) vs oesophageal (retrosternal pain a few seconds in).
  • Identify the cause, dominated by oesophagitis (infective, pill / chemical, or reflux).
  • Always ask about immunosuppression (HIV, chemotherapy, steroids) and medications.
🚨An airway emergency hides here: a patient who cannot swallow their own saliva (drooling), is febrile, with a muffled “hot-potato” voice or stridor may have epiglottitis, a peritonsillar abscess (quinsy) or a deep-neck-space infection — get senior ENT / anaesthetic help and do not distress the airway (never examine the throat in suspected epiglottitis in a child). Also urgent: caustic ingestion, and progressive odynophagia with weight loss (oesophageal cancer).

GASTROINTESTINAL__Dysphagia:
Dysphagia (difficulty swallowing) is a red-flag symptom until proven benign. Two questions solve it.
  • Where? — oropharyngeal (difficulty initiating the swallow, with coughing / choking, nasal regurgitation and a wet voice — usually neuromuscular) vs oesophageal (food sticks a few seconds after swallowing, felt retrosternally).
  • For oesophageal, what pattern? — mechanical (solids first, progressive → stricture / cancer / ring) vs motility (solids AND liquids from the start → achalasia / spasm / systemic sclerosis).
  • Always screen the red flags (urgent endoscopy) and assess aspiration risk. Painful swallowing is odynophagia (see Odynophagia).
🚨Any new dysphagia needs urgent (2-week-wait) upper-GI endoscopy — especially progressive dysphagia to solids with weight loss, anaemia, or age ≥55 (exclude oesophageal / gastric cancer). And assess the swallow’s safety: coughing / choking, a wet voice or recurrent chest infections signal an unsafe swallow with aspiration risk → keep NBM and refer to SALT.

GASTROINTESTINAL__Heartburn & Acid Regur:
Heartburn (pyrosis — a retrosternal burning worse on lying, bending or after meals) and acid regurgitation (the effortless return of acid or food to the throat / mouth) are symptoms, not a diagnosis.
  • Commonest cause is gastro-oesophageal reflux disease (GORD) — but they can be mimicked by cardiac pain and, when chronic, cause Barrett’s oesophagus and stricture.
  • Characterise the reflux symptoms (and spot the atypical / extra-oesophageal ones), and screen the red flags.
  • Step through the management ladder — lifestyle → antacid / alginate → PPI → (endoscopy) → surgery. (For epigastric pain / ulcer-type symptoms, see Dyspepsia.)
🚨Refer for urgent (2-week-wait) endoscopy if reflux is accompanied by dysphagia at any age, or age ≥55 with weight loss plus reflux / dyspepsia; and for any GI bleed / iron-deficiency anaemia, persistent vomiting or an epigastric mass. And never assume “reflux” for chest pain until you have excluded a cardiac cause — reflux is a diagnosis of exclusion for chest pain (see Chest Pain).

1Characterise it
🔍Characterise the symptoms
  • Heartburn (pyrosis): retrosternal burning, worse lying flat / bending / after large meals, relieved by antacids
  • Acid regurgitation: effortless return of acid / food to the throat or mouth (no nausea or retching)
  • Waterbrash (sudden flood of saliva) and a sour taste; symptoms are often nocturnal
🚩Red flags & the cardiac mimic
  • Dysphagia (any age), weight loss, GI bleed / anaemia, persistent vomiting, an epigastric mass → urgent endoscopy
  • New reflux at age ≥55 with weight loss → 2-week-wait OGD (exclude oesophageal / gastric cancer — see Dysphagia)
  • Exclude cardiac chest pain — do not label exertional / radiating chest pain as reflux without an ECG
⚙️Mechanism & triggers
  • A weak / transiently relaxing lower oesophageal sphincter, often with a hiatus hernia
  • Raised intra-abdominal pressure — obesity, pregnancy, tight clothing, large meals
  • Triggers: fatty / spicy food, caffeine, chocolate, alcohol, smoking, late meals, and drugs (nitrates, CCBs, anticholinergics, theophylline, beta-agonists)
👂Atypical / extra-oesophageal
  • Chronic cough, nocturnal wheeze / asthma (see Asthma), hoarseness / laryngitis
  • Globus sensation, recurrent sore throat / sinusitis, and dental erosion
  • Non-cardiac chest pain — reflux is a common cause once the heart is excluded
⚠️Complications of chronic reflux
  • Reflux oesophagitis and peptic stricture (causing dysphagia)
  • Barrett’s oesophagus (columnar metaplasia) — premalignant, raising the risk of oesophageal adenocarcinoma
  • Aspiration, chronic anaemia, and dental damage
🪜The management ladder
  • Lifestyle: weight loss, smaller / earlier meals, stop smoking, cut alcohol / caffeine, raise the bed head
  • Antacids / alginates for symptom relief, then a full-dose PPI (4–8 weeks) — the mainstay
  • Refractory / red-flag → endoscopy and pH & manometry studies; then consider anti-reflux surgery (fundoplication)
Heartburn and regurgitation are symptoms; their commonest diagnosis is GORD. The test-of-treatment is simple: no red flags → lifestyle + a PPI trial, and a good response supports GORD. Red flags or a refractory / atypical picture → scope. And first, make sure the chest pain is not the heart.

GASTROINTESTINAL__Dyspepsia & Epigastric:
Dyspepsia (“indigestion”) is a symptom complex of epigastric pain or burning, postprandial fullness, early satiety, bloating and nausea.
  • Extremely common and usually benign (functional dyspepsia, GORD, peptic ulcer) — but a small number hide an upper-GI cancer.
  • Characterise the pain, then screen the ALARM red flags that demand urgent endoscopy.
  • Decide the pathway: H. pylori test-and-treat / a PPI trial versus a scope.
  • Always exclude the cardiac, biliary and pancreatic mimics of epigastric pain (see also Abdominal Pain).
🚨Refer for urgent (2-week-wait) upper-GI endoscopy if there is dysphagia at any age, or age ≥55 with weight loss plus upper-abdominal pain / reflux / dyspepsia. The ALARMS red flags — Anaemia, Loss of weight, Anorexia, Recent onset / progressive, Melaena or haematemesis / epigastric mass, Swallowing difficulty — point to malignancy. And never forget the inferior MI that presents as “indigestion”.

  • Functional (non-ulcer) dyspepsia — the commonest, a diagnosis of exclusion with a normal scope

  • Drives most peptic ulcers and much dyspepsia; the core of the no-red-flag pathway

  • Positive → eradication triple therapy (PPI + two antibiotics, e.g. amoxicillin + clarithromycin) for 7 days

  • Review NSAIDs / aspirin, steroids, bisphosphonates and other gastric irritants — stop or add gastroprotection
  • Smoking, alcohol, caffeine, weight, late / large meals — lifestyle drives GORD and dyspepsia
  • A 4-week trial of a PPI is reasonable first-line where there are no red flags

GASTROINTESTINAL__Nausea & Vomiting:
Nausea & vomiting is one of the commonest presentations in medicine — and one of the most non-specific, because the vomiting centre in the medulla is driven from four directions:
  • The chemoreceptor trigger zone (drugs, metabolic, toxins).
  • The gut (vagal — obstruction, irritation).
  • The vestibular system (motion, labyrinthitis).
  • Higher centres (pain, smell, raised ICP).
  • Work it in three moves: characterise the vomit (content, timing, force), split central vs peripheral, and triage the red flags & complications — keep bowel obstruction, raised ICP, DKA, inferior MI and, in any woman of reproductive age, pregnancy in mind.
🚨Do not miss: bilious or faeculent vomiting → bowel obstruction; haematemesis / coffee-ground → upper-GI bleed; projectile vomiting with a morning headache or focal neurology → raised intracranial pressure; projectile vomiting in a hungry 3–6-week infant → pyloric stenosis; and the systemic killers — DKA, inferior MI, Addisonian crisis and sepsis. Severe or protracted vomiting risks dehydration, hypokalaemia, a Mallory-Weiss tear or Boerhaave’s rupture.

  • Bilious / faeculent → bowel obstruction; haematemesis / coffee-ground → upper-GI bleed
  • Projectile + morning headache / focal neurology / papilloedema → raised ICP; projectile in a hungry infant → pyloric stenosis
  • Signs of shock / severe dehydration, or vomiting with severe pain, ketones or ECG changes → a systemic emergency
🧠Central causes (CTZ / cortical / vestibular)
  • Drugs / toxins: opioids, chemotherapy, digoxin, antibiotics, alcohol
  • Metabolic: DKA, uraemia, hypercalcaemia, hyponatraemia, Addisonian crisis
  • CNS / vestibular: raised ICP, migraine, labyrinthitis / BPPV / Ménière’s; and pregnancy
🩺Peripheral / GI causes
  • Gastroenteritis (commonest), bowel obstruction, gastric outlet obstruction / gastroparesis
  • Peptic ulcer / gastritis, pancreatitis, biliary disease / cholangitis, appendicitis / peritonitis
  • Hepatitis, and GORD / achalasia (more regurgitation than true vomiting)
⚕️Don’t-miss systemic mimics
  • Inferior MI and DKA — vomiting can be the presenting feature; ECG, glucose & ketones early
  • Raised ICP (tumour, bleed, meningitis), Addisonian crisis, sepsis, hypercalcaemia
  • In any woman of reproductive age, do a pregnancy test — pregnancy & hyperemesis gravidarum

  • Dehydration & AKI; hypokalaemia + hypochloraemic metabolic alkalosis (loss of H⁺ / Cl⁻ / K⁺)

  • Assess hydration / shock, U&E, glucose, ketones, calcium, amylase, LFTs, VBG, an ECG and a βhCG

GASTROINTESTINAL__Peritonism (Guarding &:
Peritonism (peritonitis on examination) is the set of physical signs of an irritated parietal peritoneum — guarding, rigidity, rebound / percussion tenderness and pain worse on movement or coughing.
  • The single most important thing to find in abdominal pain: it separates a localised problem (an inflamed organ — appendicitis, cholecystitis, diverticulitis) from generalised peritonitis (spillage / perforation) — a surgical acute abdomen.
  • The key distinction: voluntary guarding (anticipatory, suppressible) versus involuntary guarding / rigidity (a reflex you cannot override) — the hallmark of true peritonism.
🚨A board-like rigid, generally tender, silent abdomen in a shocked patient is generalised peritonitis until proven otherwise — from perforation, ischaemic bowel or spillage of pus / blood / bowel content. Resuscitate and call surgery now; do not wait for imaging. Remember peritoneal signs may be blunted in the elderly, immunosuppressed and pregnant.

1Recognise it
🔍What peritonism is
  • Signs of an inflamed parietal peritoneum — the sensitive lining that localises pain sharply and hurts on movement
  • Localised peritonism → a single inflamed organ (appendix, gallbladder, diverticulum); generalised → spillage / perforation
  • Distinct from visceral pain (dull, midline, poorly localised) — peritonism is sharp, localised and movement-sensitive
🚩Generalised peritonitis
  • Board-like rigidity, generalised tenderness, a silent (absent bowel sounds) abdomen and shock
  • Patient lies completely still — any movement, coughing or the car journey in hurt
  • Cause = perforation / ischaemia / spillage of pus, blood or bowel content → resuscitate & call surgery — see Acute Abdomen
✋Guarding & rigidity
  • Voluntary guarding: the patient tenses in anticipation — suppressible with distraction / gentle warm hands
  • Involuntary guarding: a reflex contraction the patient cannot override — this is true peritonism
  • Rigidity (“board-like”) is sustained involuntary guarding — the most extreme, ominous form
👇Rebound & percussion tenderness
  • Rebound tenderness: pain worse on sudden release of pressure (Blumberg’s sign) — but crude and unkind
  • Percussion tenderness & the cough test: gentler, more humane and equally reliable ways to show peritoneal irritation
  • Pain on coughing, moving or the bumps in the road is peritonism until proven otherwise — prefer these to hard rebound
🎯The special localising signs
  • Rovsing’s: pressing the LIF causes RIF pain → appendicitis; psoas / obturator signs → a retrocaecal / pelvic appendix
  • Murphy’s sign: RUQ pressure arrests inspiration → cholecystitis (localised biliary peritonism)
  • Cervical excitation & adnexal tenderness → pelvic peritonism (PID, ectopic) — do a βhCG
⚕️Confirm it is peritoneal — and act
  • Carnett’s test: tenderness that worsens on tensing the abdominal wall (head-lift) is wall, not peritoneum; if it eases, it is intra-abdominal
  • Generalised peritonism → resuscitate, NBM, IV, analgesia & call surgery; localised → target the organ
  • Do a PR / pelvic exam and, in women, a βhCG; peritoneal signs are muted in the elderly / immunosuppressed / pregnant
The question is always the same: is it localised or generalised? Localised peritonism points to one inflamed organ; generalised rigidity with shock means spillage / perforation — a surgical emergency. And it is involuntary guarding / rigidity, not the voluntary kind, that proves true peritoneal irritation.

GASTROINTESTINAL__Acute Abdomen:
An acute abdomen is the surgical-emergency subset of abdominal pain — a sudden, severe abdominal condition where the pivotal question is “does this abdomen need theatre?”
  • Work it as a resus, not a work-up.
  • Recognise the surgical abdomen (peritonism — see Peritonism — and shock / sepsis).
  • Resuscitate in parallel: NBM, IV, fluids, analgesia, bloods incl. lactate & βhCG.
  • Pattern the emergency (perforation, obstruction / strangulation, ischaemia, ruptured AAA, ruptured ectopic), then decide the pathway — theatre vs conservative.
🚨A rigid, silent abdomen in a shocked patient is a surgical emergency — resuscitate and call surgery now, do not wait for imaging. Do not miss perforation (free air), strangulated obstruction / mesenteric ischaemia (pain out of proportion, high lactate), a ruptured AAA (older, back / flank pain, shock, pulsatile mass) and a ruptured ectopic (reproductive-age woman — βhCG). And beware the medical mimics (inferior MI, DKA) — do not take these to theatre.

1Recognise it
🔍Recognise a surgical abdomen
  • Sudden, severe pain in a patient who looks systemically unwell (tachycardic, hypotensive, febrile, oliguric)
  • The patient lies still (peritonitis — movement hurts) vs writhes / cannot settle (colic — obstruction, stone)
  • The pivotal question is not the exact diagnosis but “does this need theatre?” — recognise, resuscitate, refer
🚩Peritonitis — the cardinal signs
  • Rigidity (board-like, involuntary), guarding, rebound / percussion tenderness, pain on coughing / movement
  • Absent bowel sounds (ileus) with a still, tense abdomen → generalised peritonitis until proven otherwise
  • Localised → a walled-off inflamed organ (appendix, gallbladder, diverticulum); generalised → perforation / spillage — see Peritonism
💥Perforation
  • Sudden severe generalised pain, rigid silent abdomen, shock; commonest = perforated peptic ulcer
  • Erect CXR: free air under the diaphragm (absent in ~30%) — CT is more sensitive
  • Resuscitate, broad-spectrum antibiotics → theatre for washout & repair
🔄Obstruction & strangulation
  • Colicky central pain, distension, vomiting, absolute constipation; bowel sounds tinkling → then absent
  • Check every hernial orifice and old scars (adhesions) — an irreducible tender hernia is obstructing
  • Strangulation = obstruction + constant pain, tenderness, fever, tachycardia, high lactate → ischaemic bowel → theatre
🩸Vascular / haemorrhagic catastrophe
  • Ruptured AAA: older, back / flank pain, shock, pulsatile expansile mass → theatre (do not delay for CT if unstable)
  • Mesenteric ischaemia: pain out of proportion to signs, AF / vascular disease, metabolic acidosis, high lactate
  • Ruptured ectopic: reproductive-age woman, amenorrhoea, shock — βhCG on every one
⚕️The mimics — don’t take these to theatre
  • Inferior MI and DKA present with abdominal pain — ECG, glucose & ketones on arrival
  • Acute pancreatitis (raised lipase) and uncomplicated diverticulitis / cholecystitis are usually managed medically first
  • Basal pneumonia, Addisonian crisis, hypercalcaemia — a surgical-looking abdomen that a knife will not fix
Three moves carry an acute abdomen: recognise the surgical abdomen (peritonism, shock), resuscitate in parallel with assessment, and refer early. You do not need the final diagnosis to act — a rigid, shocked, silent abdomen earns a surgical review before the scan.

GASTROINTESTINAL__Abdominal Pain:
Abdominal pain is one of medicine’s biggest presentations — spanning acute or chronic, benign or life-threatening, and surgical, medical or gynaecological causes.
  • Characterise the pain: site, character, visceral vs parietal, colicky vs constant.
  • Localise it by region.
  • Triage severity: a rigid, shocked abdomen is an Acute Abdomen (see also Peritonism).
  • Always keep the medical mimics (MI, DKA) and, in any woman of reproductive age, ectopic pregnancy in mind.
🚨Do not miss the time-critical causes: peritonitis / rigid abdomen + shock (perforation, ischaemia) → resuscitate and call surgery; a ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm (older, back / flank pain, shock, pulsatile mass); mesenteric ischaemia (pain out of proportion, AF, high lactate); an ectopic pregnancy (reproductive-age woman — do a βhCG); and the medical mimics — inferior MI (epigastric pain) and DKA (diffuse abdominal pain) must always be considered.

Overview — The Muscular Conduit

The oesophagus is a ~25 cm muscular tube carrying food from the pharynx to the stomach. It has no digestive or absorptive role — it is built for abrasion resistance (a tough stratified squamous lining) and propulsion (peristalsis).

🔬 Image slot — oesophagus at low power — folded (star-shaped) lumen, the four concentric layers, and submucosal glands

It follows the general four-layer plan of the GI tract, and every hollow gut organ is read the same way — from lumen outward:

2
Submucosadense CT, vessels, glands, Meissner plexus
3
Muscularis externainner circular + outer longitudinal, Auerbach plexus
4
