Two features let you name the oesophagus at a glance: a non-keratinised stratified squamous lining and mucous glands sitting in the submucosa. Together they are almost unique to the oesophagus.
How to Recognise It on a Slide ⭐
🔬 Image slot — oesophageal wall — thick stratified squamous epithelium, lamina propria, thick muscularis mucosae, submucosal mucous glands
  • Non-keratinised stratified squamous epithelium — thick, pale, with flattened surface cells that keep their nuclei (no keratin layer).
  • Folded, star-shaped lumen — longitudinal mucosal/submucosal folds that flatten out when a bolus passes.
  • Oesophageal glands proper in the submucosa — the single best discriminator (few other places have submucosal mucous glands; the duodenum's Brunner glands are the other classic).
  • Thick muscularis mucosae of mostly longitudinal smooth muscle — unusually prominent here.
  • Adventitia, not serosa, over most of its length (a cervical/posterior-mediastinal tube with no peritoneal covering).
Stratified squamous lumen + mucous glands in the submucosa → oesophagus. If instead you see squamous epithelium with no submucosal glands, think vagina/anal canal; if you see it keratinised, think skin.
Layer 1 — Mucosa
🔬 Image slot — oesophageal mucosa — stratified squamous epithelium, lamina propria papillae, muscularis mucosae
Epithelium
  • Non-keratinised stratified squamous — protects against mechanical abrasion from food
  • Continuously renewed from a basal layer; surface cells retain nuclei
Lamina propria
  • Loose CT with vessels & immune cells
  • Contains oesophageal cardiac glands near the two ends (mucous; protect against reflux/abrasion)
  • Muscularis mucosae — here it is thick and mostly longitudinal (a useful clue); it thickens distally toward the stomach.
Two named mucous glands — don’t mix them up: cardiac glands lie in the lamina propria at the ends; glands proper lie in the submucosa along the whole length.
Layer 2 — Submucosa & the Oesophageal Glands
🔬 Image slot — submucosa — tubuloacinar mucous glands (oesophageal glands proper) with ducts crossing the muscularis mucosae, plus a venous plexus
  • Dense irregular connective tissue carrying the larger blood vessels, lymphatics and nerves.
  • Oesophageal glands proper — small tubuloacinar mucous glands scattered along the whole length; their ducts pierce the mucosa to lubricate the bolus.
  • Meissner (submucosal) plexus — autonomic ganglia controlling glandular secretion and local blood flow.
  • A longitudinal submucosal venous plexus — clinically vital (see varices below).
The distal oesophageal submucosal veins are a porto-systemic anastomosis (left gastric vein → azygos). In portal hypertension they dilate into oesophageal varices — a lethal cause of upper-GI bleeding.
Layer 3 — Muscularis Externa (the “Two-Thirds” Rule)
🔬 Image slot — muscularis externa — inner circular and outer longitudinal layers with the myenteric (Auerbach) plexus between them

Two layers — inner circular and outer longitudinal — but the muscle type changes down the length, which is a favourite exam point:

↑
Upper 1/3Skeletal (striated) muscle — voluntary start of swallowing
↔
Middle 1/3Mixed skeletal + smooth muscle
↓
Lower 1/3Smooth muscle — involuntary peristalsis
  • Myenteric (Auerbach) plexus lies between the two muscle layers and drives peristalsis.
  • Upper & lower oesophageal sphincters bracket the tube: the UOS (cricopharyngeus) is skeletal; the LOS is a physiological smooth-muscle sphincter reinforced by the diaphragmatic crura.
Loss of the myenteric ganglion cells (& interstitial cells of Cajal) in the lower oesophagus → non-relaxing LOS + lost peristalsis → achalasia (“bird’s-beak” barium, aperistalsis on manometry). Secondary: Chagas (T. cruzi) & pseudoachalasia (GOJ cancer). Rx pneumatic dilation/Heller/POEM.
Layer 4 — Adventitia vs Serosa
  • Most of the oesophagus is in the neck/thorax and is wrapped by adventitia — connective tissue that blends into surrounding mediastinal structures (no mesothelial covering).
  • Only the short abdominal segment (below the diaphragm) has a true serosa (mesothelium).
Because most of the wall lacks a serosal barrier, oesophageal tumours spread locally early and perforations leak into the mediastinum — part of why oesophageal cancer carries a poor prognosis.
The Gastro-oesophageal Junction & Barrett’s
🔬 Image slot — gastro-oesophageal junction — abrupt Z-line where stratified squamous meets gastric simple columnar epithelium
  • At the gastro-oesophageal junction the lining changes abruptly from stratified squamous to the simple columnar epithelium of the gastric cardia — the Z-line (squamocolumnar junction).
  • Barrett’s oesophagus = chronic acid reflux drives metaplasia of the squamous lining into columnar epithelium. Goblet cells (intestinal metaplasia) are required by US/ACG; UK/BSG accepts any columnar segment ≥1 cm.
Barrett’s is premalignant — the key risk factor for oesophageal adenocarcinoma. Surveillance grades: negative → indefinite → low-grade → high-grade dysplasia → intramucosal cancer; dysplasia treated by radiofrequency ablation ± EMR.
Clinical / Pathological Correlate
Reflux oesophagitis (GORD)
Basal cell hyperplasia, elongated lamina-propria papillae, and intra-epithelial eosinophils/neutrophils
Barrett’s oesophagus
Squamous → columnar + goblet-cell (intestinal) metaplasia; premalignant
Adenocarcinoma
Lower third; arises from Barrett’s; risk = GORD, obesity — commonest type in the West
Squamous cell carcinoma
Upper/middle third; risk = smoking & alcohol, also achalasia, Plummer–Vinson, hot drinks, caustic strictures, tylosis — commonest worldwide
Oesophageal varices
Dilated distal submucosal veins (portal HTN) → catastrophic bleed. Rx: terlipressin + antibiotics, band ligation, TIPS; prophylaxis = non-selective β-blocker/banding.
Achalasia
Loss of myenteric plexus ganglion cells → non-relaxing LOS & failed peristalsis
Eosinophilic oesophagitis
Allergic; >15 eosinophils/hpf, rings & furrows; dysphagia in young atopic patients (Rx PPI/diet/topical steroid)
Infective oesophagitis
Immunocompromised: Candida (plaques, pseudohyphae), HSV (punched-out ulcers, Cowdry A, squamous edge), CMV (linear ulcers, owl-eye, endothelium).
Plummer–Vinson
Oesophageal web + iron-deficiency anaemia + glossitis/dysphagia; women; premalignant for postcricoid SCC.
Mallory–Weiss vs Boerhaave
Mallory–Weiss = mucosal GOJ tear after vomiting → haematemesis (self-limiting). Boerhaave = full-thickness rupture → mediastinitis, surgical emergency.
⭐ Exam Pearls
Non-keratinised stratified squamous + submucosal mucous glands = oesophagus.
Four layers, read lumen-outward: mucosa → submucosa → muscularis externa → adventitia.
Muscularis externa muscle type: upper 1/3 skeletal, middle mixed, lower 1/3 smooth.
Glands proper = submucosa, whole length (lubrication); cardiac glands = lamina propria, at the two ends.
Auerbach (myenteric) plexus lies between the muscle layers (peristalsis); Meissner (submucosal) plexus controls glands/secretion.
Adventitia, not serosa, over most of its length → early local spread of tumours.
Z-line = abrupt squamous→columnar junction; Barrett’s = squamous→columnar+goblet metaplasia → adenocarcinoma.
SCC = upper/middle, smoking & alcohol; adenocarcinoma = lower third, Barrett’s/GORD.
Varices = submucosal veins in portal hypertension; achalasia = loss of myenteric ganglion cells.
GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (layers, gland:
Overview — The Acid-Secreting Mixing Sac

The stomach mixes food, secretes acid and enzymes, and begins protein digestion, turning the bolus into chyme. It keeps the four-layer GI plan but with three signature modifications: a simple columnar lining dipping into gastric pits, an extra (oblique) muscle layer, and mucosal folds called rugae.

🔬 Image slot — stomach at low power — simple columnar surface dipping into gastric pits, glands filling the mucosa, three muscle layers

It has four regions, and their glands differ — a favourite exam theme:

Cardia & Pylorus (antrum)
  • Deep pits, short coiled mucous glands
  • Pylorus is rich in G cells (gastrin)
Fundus & Body
  • Oxyntic (gastric) glands — the workhorse
  • Contain parietal + chief cells → acid & pepsinogen
Read the stomach in two steps: confirm it is stomach (columnar + pits, no goblet cells, no villi), then decide the region by which cells fill the glands.
How to Recognise It on a Slide ⭐
🔬 Image slot — gastric mucosa — surface mucous cells, gastric pits, and glands packed with pink parietal and blue chief cells
  • Simple columnar surface epithelium that dips into gastric pits (foveolae) — the glands open at the pit base.
  • No goblet cells and no villi — this separates stomach from intestine at a glance.
  • In body/fundus: glands packed with pink (eosinophilic) parietal cells and blue (basophilic) chief cells.
  • In antrum/pylorus: deep pits over short, coiled, pale mucous glands (few/no parietal cells).
Columnar epithelium + gastric pits, but no goblet cells and no villi → stomach. The moment you see goblet cells or villi you are in intestine (or looking at intestinal metaplasia).
The Pit–Gland Unit
🔬 Image slot — the gastric pit-gland unit — pit (foveola), isthmus, neck (stem cells), and gland base

Each functional unit runs surface → base:

1
Gastric pit (foveola)lined by surface mucous cells
2
Isthmus / neckstem cells + mucous neck cells
3
Gland (body & base)parietal, chief & enteroendocrine cells
  • The pit : gland ratio maps region: deep pits/short glands in cardia & pylorus; short pits/long glands in body & fundus.
  • Stem cells in the isthmus/neck renew the epithelium — upward into the pit and downward into the gland.
The Five Cell Types (High-Yield)
Surface & neck mucous cells
Surface cells make an insoluble alkaline (bicarbonate-rich) gel — the protective barrier; neck cells (stem-cell zone) make a distinct soluble, more acidic mucin
Parietal (oxyntic) cells
Pink/eosinophilic, “fried-egg”, central nucleus; secrete HCl (H⁺/K⁺ ATPase) & intrinsic factor; upper/mid gland
Chief (zymogenic) cells
Blue/basophilic base (RER) + apical zymogen granules; secrete pepsinogen & gastric lipase; gland base
Enteroendocrine cells
G cells (gastrin, antrum), ECL cells (histamine), D cells (somatostatin); at the gland base
Stem cells
In the isthmus/neck; renew all gastric epithelial cells
Parietal = Pink
  • Acid (HCl) + intrinsic factor
  • Round, central nucleus, canaliculi
  • Higher up the gland
Chief = Blue
  • Pepsinogen (→ pepsin in acid)
  • Basophilic basal cytoplasm
  • Deep at the gland base
Parietal Pink, Chief Chromatic-blue. Parietal cells make the two P’s — Proton (acid) and Protein-binder for B12 (intrinsic factor).
Acid Secretion & Its Control
🔬 Image slot — parietal cell — canaliculi, H+/K+ ATPase proton pump, and the gastrin / histamine / ACh inputs
  • The H⁺/K⁺ ATPase (proton pump) on the parietal-cell canaliculi pumps out H⁺ — the final common step and the target of PPIs.
  • Carbonic anhydrase supplies the H⁺ (and HCO₃⁻); bicarbonate exiting the base into blood is the post-prandial alkaline tide. On stimulation, cytoplasmic tubulovesicles fuse into the canaliculus, hugely expanding the pump-bearing membrane.
  • Stimulate acid: gastrin (G cells), histamine (ECL cells, via H₂ receptors), ACh (vagus).
  • Inhibit acid: somatostatin (D cells) — low luminal pH stimulates D cells, whose somatostatin restrains both G cells and parietal cells (the negative-feedback loop); duodenal enterogastrones (secretin, GIP, CCK) also damp acid.
  • Intrinsic factor from parietal cells binds B12 for absorption in the terminal ileum.
Drug targets follow the biology: PPIs block the proton pump; H₂-blockers (ranitidine-type) block the histamine input; loss of parietal cells removes both acid and intrinsic factor.
Mucosal Barrier & the Extra Muscle Layer
Gastric mucosal barrier
  • Mucus–bicarbonate layer + surface tight junctions
  • Prostaglandins maintain mucus & blood flow
  • Rapid epithelial turnover
Muscularis externa
  • Three layers: inner oblique, middle circular, outer longitudinal
  • The extra oblique layer enables churning
  • Circular layer thickens at the pyloric sphincter
NSAIDs inhibit prostaglandin synthesis → a weakened mucus/bicarbonate barrier → erosions and peptic ulcers.
Clinical / Pathological Correlate
H. pylori gastritis
Curved urease⁺ bacilli (CagA/VacA). Antral-predominant → ↓somatostatin → ↑gastrin/↑acid → duodenal ulcer; corpus/pan-gastritis → atrophy/↓acid → gastric ulcer, metaplasia & cancer. Dx: urease/CLO, urea breath, stool antigen.
Peptic ulcer disease
Mucosal breach (H. pylori / NSAIDs); duodenal > gastric; bleeding (posterior DU → gastroduodenal artery) & perforation. Gastric ulcers must be biopsied to exclude cancer. Stress ulcers: Curling (burns), Cushing (raised ICP).
Autoimmune (atrophic) gastritis
Anti-parietal & anti-IF antibodies → loss of parietal cells (body/fundus) → achlorhydria + pernicious anaemia (B12; can give SACD). Achlorhydria → hypergastrinaemia → ECL hyperplasia → type 1 gastric carcinoid.
Intestinal metaplasia
Goblet cells appear in gastric mucosa → a premalignant change toward adenocarcinoma
Gastric adenocarcinoma
Intestinal type (glands, on metaplasia) vs diffuse type (signet-ring cells, linitis plastica, CDH1/E-cadherin loss). Spread: Virchow node (Troisier), Krukenberg ovary, Sister Mary Joseph nodule.
Zollinger–Ellison
Gastrinoma → parietal-cell hyperplasia, high acid & refractory/distal ulcers ± diarrhoea; secretin stimulation test (paradoxical ↑gastrin); ~25% part of MEN1.
Gastric MALT lymphoma
H. pylori-driven marginal-zone B-cell lymphoma; often regresses with eradication — but t(11;18) predicts failure to respond.
GIST
Mesenchymal tumour of the interstitial cells of Cajal; c-KIT (CD117) positive
Infantile pyloric stenosis
Pyloric circular-muscle hypertrophy at 3–6 weeks → non-bilious projectile vomiting, palpable ‘olive’, hypochloraemic hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis; Ramstedt pyloromyotomy.
Ménétrier disease
Giant rugal hypertrophy (foveolar hyperplasia, TGF-α) → protein-losing gastropathy & hypochlorhydria; rare, premalignant.
⭐ Exam Pearls
Simple columnar + gastric pits, no goblet cells, no villi = stomach.
Parietal Pink (HCl + intrinsic factor, upper gland); Chief blue (pepsinogen, gland base).
Body/fundus = oxyntic glands (parietal + chief); antrum = G cells making gastrin.
H⁺/K⁺ ATPase (proton pump) = PPI target; acid driven by gastrin, histamine (ECL) & ACh, inhibited by somatostatin (D cells).
Stomach has three muscle layers (extra inner oblique) for churning.
Autoimmune gastritis destroys parietal cells → no intrinsic factor → B12 deficiency (pernicious anaemia).
H. pylori → antral gastritis, peptic ulcers, MALT lymphoma & adenocarcinoma.
Intestinal metaplasia (goblet cells in stomach) is premalignant; diffuse carcinoma = signet-ring cells & linitis plastica.
NSAIDs block prostaglandins → weakened mucus/bicarbonate barrier → ulcers.
GASTROINTESTINAL__Small Intestine (villi:
Overview — Built for Surface Area

The small intestine (duodenum → jejunum → ileum) is the main site of digestion and absorption. Its entire design is about maximising surface area — three tiers of folding amplify it ~600-fold:

🔬 Image slot — small intestine at low power — plicae circulares thrown into finger-like villi, with crypts between their bases
1
Plicae circularespermanent folds of mucosa + submucosa (valves of Kerckring)
2
Villifinger-like mucosal projections
3
Microvillithe brush border on each enterocyte
Villi are unique to the small intestine (found nowhere else in the gut); the diagnostic pairing is villi + crypts of Lieberkühn between their bases. Crypts alone also occur in the colon — but the colon has no villi.
How to Recognise It on a Slide ⭐
🔬 Image slot — small-intestinal mucosa — villi lined by simple columnar enterocytes with a brush border and interspersed goblet cells, crypts at the base
  • Villi (projections) + crypts of Lieberkühn (invaginations) — the diagnostic pairing.
  • Simple columnar epithelium with a pink apical brush border (microvilli) and scattered goblet cells.
  • A lacteal (central lymphatic) runs up the core of each villus.
Villi + crypts + goblet cells + brush border → small intestine. Then decide which part by looking for Brunner glands (duodenum) or Peyer’s patches (ileum).
Telling the Three Parts Apart
🔬 Image slot — comparison — duodenum with submucosal Brunner glands, jejunum with tall villi & plicae, ileum with Peyer's patches
Duodenum
Brunner glands in the submucosa (the only intestinal submucosal glands — the oesophagus also has submucosal glands) — alkaline mucus that neutralises gastric acid; broad, leaf-shaped villi
Jejunum
Tall, finger-like villi and the tallest plicae circulares; no Brunner glands, few lymphoid aggregates
Ileum
Peyer’s patches (large lymphoid aggregates); shorter villi and the most goblet cells
Landmarks: Brunner glands = duodenum; Peyer’s patches = ileum. Goblet cells steadily increase from duodenum to ileum.
The Cell Types (High-Yield)
Enterocytes
Tall columnar absorptive cells with an apical brush border of microvilli + glycocalyx carrying digestive enzymes
Goblet cells
Secrete lubricating mucus; increase in number toward the ileum
Paneth cells
At the crypt base; bright eosinophilic apical granules; secrete lysozyme & defensins (antimicrobial) and guard the stem cells
Enteroendocrine cells
Scattered: I=CCK, S=secretin, K=GIP, L=GLP-1/PYY, EC=serotonin, D=somatostatin
Stem cells
At the crypt base (Lgr5⁺); continually renew the epithelium (turnover ~3–5 days)
M (microfold) cells
Overlie Peyer’s patches; sample luminal antigen and pass it to immune cells
Paneth cells sit at the crypt base with the stem cells — their eosinophilic granules are a giveaway. They are the only crypt-base secretory cell you can spot on H&E.
The Crypt–Villus Axis
🔬 Image slot — crypt-villus axis — proliferation in the crypt, migration up the villus, and shedding at the tip
Crypt = proliferation
  • Houses stem cells & Paneth cells
  • New cells are born here and migrate upward
Villus = absorption
  • Mature enterocytes & goblet cells
  • Old cells are shed from the tip (anoikis)
  • Each villus core (lamina propria) carries a central lacteal (lymphatic) for fat/chylomicron absorption, a capillary network for other nutrients, and a strand of smooth muscle that “milks” the lacteal.
This rapid turnover is why the gut lining is so vulnerable to chemotherapy/radiation (mucositis) — and why coeliac damage is crypt hyperplasia with villous atrophy (the crypts work overtime to replace lost surface).
Absorption & Gut Immunity
  • Brush-border enzymes (disaccharidases, peptidases) finish carbohydrate & protein digestion at the surface.
  • Apical uptake: glucose/galactose via SGLT1 (Na⁺-coupled), fructose via GLUT5, both exiting basolaterally through GLUT2; peptides via PepT1. Duodenal enterokinase activates trypsinogen → trypsin, firing the pancreatic protease cascade.
  • Fat: micelles → enterocyte → repackaged as chylomicrons → enter the lacteal.
  • Site-specific absorption: iron & folate proximally (duodenum/jejunum); B12 (with intrinsic factor) & bile salts in the terminal ileum.
  • GALT: Peyer’s patches + M cells + lamina-propria plasma cells producing secretory IgA.
Terminal ileum resection/disease (e.g. Crohn’s) → B12 deficiency and bile-salt malabsorption — a classic exam consequence.
Clinical / Pathological Correlate
Coeliac disease
Villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia & intra-epithelial lymphocytes (Marsh) on D2 biopsy while on gluten. Anti-tTG IgA + total IgA; HLA-DQ2/DQ8. Assoc: dermatitis herpetiformis, T1DM; risk of EATL.
Crohn’s disease
Transmural inflammation, non-caseating granulomas, skip lesions; loves the terminal ileum
Whipple disease
Lamina propria stuffed with PAS-positive macrophages (Tropheryma whipplei)
Lactose intolerance
Brush-border lactase deficiency → osmotic diarrhoea & bloating (normal histology)
Meckel’s diverticulum
True ileal diverticulum (persistent vitelline duct); ectopic gastric (or pancreatic) mucosa → painless bleeding; Tc-99m pertechnetate scan. Rule of 2s.
Neuroendocrine (carcinoid) tumour
Often the ileum; serotonin → carcinoid syndrome (flushing, diarrhoea, wheeze) only with hepatic mets. Screen urinary 5-HIAA; right-heart valve fibrosis (TR/PS); Rx octreotide.
Bacterial overgrowth (SIBO)
Stasis (diverticula, strictures) → excess bacteria: classically low B12 but HIGH folate (bacteria consume B12, make folate); bloating, steatorrhoea; hydrogen breath test.
Tropical sprue / giardiasis
Tropical sprue: villous atrophy of the whole small bowel (both B12 & folate fall), Rx tetracycline + folate. Giardia: surface trophozoites → greasy diarrhoea.
⭐ Exam Pearls
Villi + crypts of Lieberkühn + goblet cells + brush border = small intestine.
Surface-area tiers: plicae circulares → villi → microvilli (~600×).
Brunner glands in the submucosa = duodenum only (alkaline mucus).
Peyer’s patches = ileum; goblet cells increase duodenum → ileum.
Paneth cells sit at the crypt base (eosinophilic granules; lysozyme/defensins, protect stem cells).
Each villus has a central lacteal for fat/chylomicron absorption.
B12 + intrinsic factor and bile salts are absorbed in the terminal ileum.
Coeliac = villous atrophy + crypt hyperplasia + intra-epithelial lymphocytes.
Crohn’s = transmural + non-caseating granulomas, terminal ileum; Meckel’s = ectopic gastric mucosa.
GASTROINTESTINAL__Large Intestine:
Overview — The Water-Reclaiming Tube

The large intestine (caecum → colon → rectum → anal canal) absorbs water and electrolytes, compacts and stores faeces, and secretes copious mucus for lubrication. It does little digestion.

🔬 Image slot — large intestine at low power — flat luminal surface (no villi) with long straight crypts packed with goblet cells

It keeps the four-layer plan but drops the small-intestinal absorptive machinery and adds a distinctive muscle arrangement:

Lost vs small intestine
  • No villi — a flat surface
  • No plicae circulares, no prominent brush border
Gained / distinctive
  • Long straight crypts full of goblet cells
  • Outer muscle condensed into taeniae coli → haustra
No villi is the single quickest discriminator: the small intestine has villi, the large intestine does not.
How to Recognise It on a Slide ⭐
🔬 Image slot — colonic mucosa — flat surface, straight test-tube crypts of Lieberkuhn densely packed with goblet cells
  • Flat luminal surface — no villi.
  • Long, straight, closely packed crypts (“test-tube” crypts of Lieberkühn) reaching down to the muscularis mucosae.
  • Abundant goblet cells lining the crypts — even more than the ileum.
  • Simple columnar epithelium of colonocytes + goblet cells.
No villi + straight crypts stuffed with goblet cells → large intestine. Add the naked-eye clue of taeniae coli & haustra and it is unmistakable.
Cell Types
Colonocytes
Absorptive cells; reclaim Na⁺ mainly by electroneutral NHE3 & SCFA-coupled uptake (ENaC/aldosterone only distally), water following osmotically; fuelled by butyrate
Goblet cells
Very abundant; secrete mucus to lubricate the increasingly solid stool
Enteroendocrine cells
Scattered hormone-secreting cells at the crypt base
Stem cells
At the crypt base; renew the epithelium (no true villus to climb)
Paneth cells are normally absent in the distal colon (a few exist in the caecum/proximal colon). Finding Paneth cells distally = Paneth-cell metaplasia, a marker of chronic mucosal injury (e.g. IBD).
The Wall & the Taeniae Coli
🔬 Image slot — colonic wall — mucosa, submucosa, inner circular muscle and the condensed outer longitudinal band (taenia coli)
  • Mucosa & submucosa as usual; submucosa carries vessels & the Meissner plexus.
  • Muscularis externa: the inner circular layer is complete, but the outer longitudinal layer condenses into three bands — the taeniae coli.
  • Because the taeniae are shorter than the gut tube, the wall puckers into sacculations called haustra; fatty tags (appendices epiploicae) hang from the surface.
  • Outer coat: serosa where intraperitoneal (transverse/sigmoid); adventitia where retroperitoneal (ascending/descending) and around the rectum.
Taeniae coli, haustra and appendices epiploicae are the three naked-eye hallmarks of colon — and the taeniae converge at the base of the appendix, a surgical landmark.
Appendix, Rectum & the Anal Canal
🔬 Image slot — anal canal — the pectinate (dentate) line where rectal simple columnar meets anal stratified squamous epithelium
  • Appendix: colon-like crypts but a small, often irregular lumen and abundant lymphoid tissue in the wall.
  • Rectum: like colon with even longer crypts and more goblet cells.

The anal canal straddles the pectinate (dentate) line — the old hindgut/proctodeum junction, and a classic exam divide:

Above pectinate line
  • Simple columnar epithelium
  • Visceral (autonomic) — insensate to pain
  • Superior rectal vein → portal; internal iliac nodes
Below pectinate line
  • Stratified squamous epithelium
  • Somatic (inferior rectal nerve) — pain-sensitive
  • Inferior rectal vein → systemic; superficial inguinal nodes
Internal anal sphincter = smooth muscle (involuntary); external anal sphincter = skeletal muscle (voluntary).
Clinical / Pathological Correlate
Ulcerative colitis
Mucosal-only, continuous from the rectum; crypt abscesses, crypt distortion, goblet-cell depletion; no granulomas. Pseudopolyps, backwash ileitis; complications: toxic megacolon, PSC (p-ANCA), ↑colorectal cancer (surveillance).
Crohn’s disease
Transmural, skip lesions, non-caseating granulomas — the contrast to UC. Cobblestoning, creeping fat, fistulae/strictures, string sign; smoking worsens (protective in UC).
Colorectal adenocarcinoma
Gland-forming; adenoma–carcinoma sequence (APC→KRAS→TP53) or serrated pathway (BRAF, CIMP, MSI, right-sided). Right = anaemia; left = obstruction/PR bleed. CEA for surveillance.
Adenomatous / serrated polyps
Tubular vs villous (villous = more risk); sessile serrated lesions (BRAF/MSI) premalignant vs benign hyperplastic. FAP (APC, >100 polyps, prophylactic colectomy); Lynch (MMR/MSI, right-sided).
Pseudomembranous colitis
C. difficile (toxins A/B); volcano-like pseudomembranes after antibiotics (clindamycin, cephalosporins); Rx oral vancomycin/fidaxomicin, FMT for recurrence.
Hirschsprung disease
Absent ganglion cells (submucosal & myenteric plexuses) in the distal colon/rectum → functional obstruction. Failed neural-crest migration (RET); Down syndrome; failure to pass meconium; Dx rectal suction biopsy (↑AChE).
Diverticular disease
False (pseudo)diverticula — mucosa + submucosa herniate through the muscularis where vasa recta pierce; sigmoid. Complications: diverticulitis (LIF pain), bleeding, fistula.
Melanosis coli
Benign, reversible brown lipofuscin pigment in lamina-propria macrophages (from apoptotic colonocytes) with chronic anthraquinone laxatives
Ischaemic colitis
Watershed splenic flexure (SMA/IMA border) & rectosigmoid; elderly, sudden LIF pain + bloody diarrhoea; thumbprinting. Rectum spared (dual supply).
Angiodysplasia
Tortuous submucosal veins in the caecum/right colon of the elderly → painless lower-GI bleed; assoc. aortic stenosis (Heyde).
Anal canal cancer is predominantly HPV-related squamous cell carcinoma arising in/around the transition zone (risk: HPV-16, HIV/immunosuppression, smoking); treated with chemoradiation (Nigro). Colorectal-type adenocarcinoma can arise above the line.
⭐ Exam Pearls
No villi + straight crypts packed with goblet cells = large intestine.
Naked-eye hallmarks: taeniae coli (3 longitudinal bands) → haustra + appendices epiploicae.
Colonocytes reclaim Na⁺ (NHE3 + SCFA-coupled; ENaC/aldosterone distally), water following osmotically; fuelled by butyrate. Goblet cells very abundant.
Paneth cells are normally absent distally; their appearance = metaplasia of chronic injury (IBD).
Pectinate line: above = columnar, visceral/insensate, portal drainage; below = squamous, somatic/painful, systemic drainage.
UC = mucosal, continuous, crypt abscesses, no granulomas; Crohn’s = transmural + granulomas + skip lesions.
Hirschsprung = absent ganglion cells in the distal bowel (RET); diverticula form where vasa recta pierce the wall.
Colorectal cancer follows the adenoma–carcinoma sequence (APC → KRAS → TP53); villous adenomas carry more risk.
Internal anal sphincter = smooth/involuntary; external = skeletal/voluntary.
GASTROINTESTINAL__Liver (lobule, sinusoi:
Overview — A Factory With a Double Blood Supply

The liver is the largest internal organ and a metabolic hub — it handles metabolism, detoxification, protein synthesis, storage and bile production. Uniquely it has a dual blood supply:

🔬 Image slot — liver at low power — hexagonal lobules with central veins and portal triads at the corners
Portal vein (~75% flow)
  • Nutrient-rich, partially deoxygenated gut blood
  • ~75% of flow but only ~50% of the O₂; delivers nutrients & toxins for first-pass processing
Hepatic artery (~25% flow)
  • Oxygenated systemic blood
  • Only ~25% of flow but ~50% of the O₂
Hepatocytes are arranged in plates radiating around a central vein, with blood-filled sinusoids between the plates. Blood flows inward to the central vein; bile flows outward to the portal triad — opposite directions.
How to Recognise It on a Slide ⭐
🔬 Image slot — hepatic lobule — plates of hepatocytes radiating from a central vein, sinusoids between them, a portal triad at the corner
  • Central vein in the middle with plates of hepatocytes radiating outward like spokes.
  • Sinusoids (wide, blood-filled capillaries) running between the plates.
  • Portal triads at the corners of the lobule — each with a portal vein branch, hepatic artery branch and bile duct.
  • Hepatocytes = large polygonal cells, eosinophilic granular cytoplasm, round central nuclei (often binucleate).
Central vein at the centre + portal triads at the corners → classic liver lobule. Find one triad and confirm its three structures to be sure.
Three Ways to Divide the Liver
🔬 Image slot — classic lobule vs portal lobule vs liver acinus — three overlapping models of hepatic architecture
Classic lobule
Hexagonal; central vein at the centre, portal triads at the corners. The structural unit
Portal lobule
Triangular; portal triad at the centre, central veins at the corners. Emphasises bile drainage (exocrine)
Liver acinus (of Rappaport)
Diamond-shaped; based on blood supply. Defines the metabolic zones 1–3 and the oxygen gradient
What is a portal triad? A portal vein branch + a hepatic artery branch + a bile duct (plus lymphatics and nerves) — remember the mnemonic that it is a triad of three tubes.
The Sinusoid & Its Cells
🔬 Image slot — hepatic sinusoid — fenestrated endothelium, Kupffer cell in the lumen, space of Disse with a stellate (Ito) cell
  • Fenestrated, discontinuous endothelium with no basement membrane — allows free exchange of plasma with hepatocytes.
  • Kupffer cells — resident macrophages in the sinusoidal lumen; remove old red cells, bacteria and debris.
  • Space of Disse — the perisinusoidal gap between endothelium and hepatocytes; site of exchange, lined by hepatocyte microvilli.
  • Hepatic stellate (Ito) cells — in the space of Disse; store vitamin A (fat); when activated become myofibroblasts that drive fibrosis.
Stellate (Ito) cell activation is the key event in cirrhosis — they switch from vitamin-A storage to collagen deposition in the space of Disse, and the sinusoids “capillarise” (gain a basement membrane), impairing exchange.
Bile Flow — the Opposite Direction
1
Bile canaliculigrooves between adjacent hepatocytes
2
Canals of Heringhepatocyte–cholangiocyte junction (stem-cell niche)
3
Bile ductules → bile ductin the portal triad
Blood flows inward (triad → central vein); bile flows outward (hepatocyte → canaliculi → triad). They move in opposite directions within the same plate — a favourite exam point.
The Metabolic Zones (High-Yield)
🔬 Image slot — the liver acinus zones — zone 1 periportal (O2-rich) through zone 2 to zone 3 centrilobular (O2-poor)
Zone 1 — Periportal
  • Nearest the triad; highest O₂ & nutrients
  • Oxidative metabolism, gluconeogenesis, β-oxidation, urea & bile
  • First to regenerate; hit first by viral hepatitis & ingested toxins; last to die in ischaemia
Zone 3 — Centrilobular
  • Nearest the central vein; lowest O₂
  • CYP450 detoxification, glycolysis, lipogenesis
  • Most vulnerable to ischaemia, paracetamol/CCl₄ toxicity and venous congestion
Zone 3 sits at the end of the oxygen gradient, so it takes the first hit from shock/ischaemia (centrilobular necrosis) and from paracetamol overdose (its CYP450 makes the toxic metabolite NAPQI). Venous congestion here gives the “nutmeg liver”.
Clinical / Pathological Correlate
Cirrhosis
Bridging fibrosis + regenerative nodules from chronic injury; driven by activated stellate cells
Centrilobular (zone 3) necrosis
Ischaemia/shock, right heart failure congestion (nutmeg liver), or paracetamol overdose
Viral hepatitis
Ballooning, apoptotic Councilman bodies, lobular/portal inflammation. A/E faeco-oral (self-limiting; E severe in pregnancy); B/C blood-borne → chronicity, cirrhosis, HCC.
Alcoholic / fatty liver disease
Zone 3 steatosis, Mallory–Denk bodies, neutrophils, perivenular fibrosis. AST:ALT >2 in alcohol; NAFLD/NASH (metabolic syndrome) is now the commonest chronic liver disease.
Hepatocellular carcinoma
On cirrhosis / HBV (can be pre-cirrhotic) / HCV / aflatoxin (p53); raised AFP; 6-monthly USS surveillance in cirrhosis.
Iron & copper overload
Haemochromatosis (HFE C282Y; Prussian-blue iron; ↑ferritin/transferrin sat, bronze diabetes; venesection). Wilson (young; ↓ceruloplasmin, Kayser-Fleischer rings; penicillamine).
α1-antitrypsin deficiency
PAS-positive, diastase-resistant globules in periportal hepatocytes; cirrhosis + early panacinar emphysema.
PBC vs PSC
PBC: AMA+, middle-aged women, small intrahepatic duct loss, itch. PSC: UC-associated, beaded ducts on MRCP, onion-skin fibrosis, ↑cholangiocarcinoma.
Budd-Chiari syndrome
Hepatic vein outflow obstruction (prothrombotic, e.g. JAK2/polycythaemia) → centrilobular congestion, painful hepatomegaly + ascites.
Portal hypertension (ascites: SAAG ≥11 g/L) opens porto-systemic anastomoses → oesophageal varices, caput medusae, rectal varices; plus splenomegaly, hepatic encephalopathy (↑ammonia; lactulose/rifaximin), SBP & hepatorenal syndrome. Severity: Child-Pugh / MELD.
⭐ Exam Pearls
Central vein at the centre + portal triads at the corners = classic liver lobule.
Portal triad = portal vein + hepatic artery + bile duct (dual supply: portal vein ~75%, hepatic artery ~25%).
Blood flows inward (triad → central vein); bile flows outward (hepatocyte → canaliculi → triad).
Zone 1 (periportal): O₂-rich; viral hepatitis & ingested toxins; regenerates first, dies last in ischaemia.
Zone 3 (centrilobular): O₂-poor; CYP450 detox; first hit by ischaemia, paracetamol and congestion (nutmeg liver).
Kupffer = sinusoidal macrophage; stellate (Ito) = vitamin-A store that drives fibrosis when activated.
Space of Disse lies between fenestrated endothelium (no basement membrane) and hepatocytes.
Cirrhosis = bridging fibrosis + regenerative nodules; HCC arises on it (raised AFP).
GASTROINTESTINAL__Gallbladder:
Overview — The Bile Reservoir

The gallbladder does not make bile — it stores and concentrates it (up to ~10-fold) between meals, then contracts to expel it after a fatty meal. Its histology is simple and stripped-down, which is exactly what makes it recognisable.

🔬 Image slot — gallbladder at low power — tall simple columnar epithelium thrown into branching mucosal folds over a single muscle layer
Its wall has only three layers — mucosa, muscularis, and perimuscular (subserosal) connective tissue — and famously lacks a muscularis mucosae and a submucosa.
How to Recognise It on a Slide ⭐
🔬 Image slot — gallbladder mucosa — tall columnar cells with apical microvilli, deep branching folds, and no goblet cells or muscularis mucosae
  • Tall simple columnar epithelium with apical microvilli (absorptive), and no goblet cells normally.
  • Highly folded mucosa — deep branching folds when the gallbladder is empty (they flatten when full).
  • No muscularis mucosae and no submucosa — the lamina propria sits straight on the muscle.
  • A single, disorganised (interlacing) smooth-muscle layer rather than distinct circular/longitudinal coats.
Tall columnar + deep mucosal folds, but no muscularis mucosae and no submucosa → gallbladder. The mucosal folds mimic villi but are irregular ridges, not the uniform finger-like villi of small bowel.
The Wall — What’s There and What’s Missing
🔬 Image slot — gallbladder wall — mucosa, single interlacing muscularis, perimuscular connective tissue, and serosa/adventitia
1
Mucosasimple columnar epithelium + lamina propria, thrown into folds
2
Muscularissingle interlacing smooth-muscle layer
3
Perimuscular / serosaconnective tissue; serosa on the free surface
  • Perimuscular (subserosal) connective tissue carries the vessels, lymphatics and nerves.
  • Serosa covers the surface hanging free from the liver; an adventitia binds the surface attached to the liver bed.
Two classic omissions: no muscularis mucosae and no submucosa — a favourite way to distinguish the gallbladder from the gut tube.
Concentrating Bile & Emptying (CCK)
  • Concentration: the columnar cells actively absorb Na⁺ (with Cl⁻ and water following), concentrating bile salts, cholesterol and pigment several-fold.
  • Emptying: a fatty/protein meal releases CCK from duodenal I cells → gallbladder contraction + relaxation of the sphincter of Oddi, delivering bile to the duodenum.
  • The epithelium also secretes a little mucus.
Because it removes water and concentrates the bile, the gallbladder is where gallstones tend to form — concentrating cholesterol or pigment past their solubility.
Rokitansky–Aschoff Sinuses & Ducts of Luschka
🔬 Image slot — Rokitansky-Aschoff sinuses — epithelial outpouchings herniating into the muscularis in chronic cholecystitis
  • Rokitansky–Aschoff sinuses — outpouchings of mucosal epithelium that herniate into/through the muscularis; the defining feature of adenomyomatosis and prominent in chronic cholecystitis/raised pressure.
  • Ducts of Luschka — small accessory bile ductules in the gallbladder-bed connective tissue; if missed at cholecystectomy they cause a post-operative bile leak.
Rokitansky–Aschoff sinuses are characteristic of, but not exclusive to, chronic cholecystitis — they define adenomyomatosis and occur in normal gallbladders. The true hallmark of chronic cholecystitis is transmural chronic inflammation with mural fibrosis & muscle hypertrophy.
Clinical / Pathological Correlate
Gallstones (cholelithiasis)
Cholesterol/mixed vs pigment: black (haemolysis/cirrhosis, in GB) vs brown (duct infection/stasis). Risk: 5 Fs + oestrogen, rapid weight loss, TPN, octreotide, ileal Crohn’s.
Biliary colic vs cholecystitis
Colic = transient post-fatty-meal pain, no fever. Cholecystitis = stone in neck/Hartmann’s pouch → persistent pain, fever, Murphy’s sign; USS first-line (HIDA if equivocal); early lap chole.
Chronic cholecystitis
Wall fibrosis, muscle hypertrophy and Rokitansky–Aschoff sinuses
Cholesterolosis (strawberry GB)
Cholesterol-laden macrophages in the lamina propria → yellow speckling on a red mucosa
Porcelain gallbladder
Calcified, fibrotic wall from chronic inflammation; a cancer risk factor (modern risk modest, ~2–6%, greatest with stippled mucosal calcification)
Gallbladder adenocarcinoma
Linked to gallstones, porcelain GB & polyps >1 cm; direct liver (seg IVb/V) invasion → late, poor prognosis
Ascending cholangitis
Infected obstructed CBD (E. coli); Charcot triad (RUQ pain, fever, jaundice), Reynolds pentad (+ hypotension, confusion). Rx antibiotics + urgent ERCP.
Mirizzi syndrome
Stone in Hartmann’s pouch/cystic duct compresses the common hepatic duct → obstructive jaundice; mimics malignancy, raises CBD-injury risk.
Gallstone ileus
Large stone erodes a cholecysto-enteric fistula → SBO (ileocaecal valve). Rigler triad: pneumobilia + SBO + ectopic stone.
Acalculous cholecystitis
GB inflammation without stones in the critically ill (sepsis, burns, TPN); stasis/ischaemia → high gangrene/perforation risk.
Courvoisier’s law: a palpable, non-tender gallbladder with painless jaundice is unlikely to be gallstones — suspect malignant obstruction (e.g. pancreatic head cancer).
⭐ Exam Pearls
Tall simple columnar + deep mucosal folds + NO muscularis mucosae + NO submucosa = gallbladder.
It stores & concentrates bile (~10×) — it does not make it.
Concentration is by active Na⁺ absorption; Cl⁻ and water follow passively (osmotically, via aquaporins).
CCK (duodenal I cells, released by fat) → gallbladder contraction + sphincter of Oddi relaxation.
Single interlacing smooth-muscle layer (no distinct circular/longitudinal coats).
Rokitansky–Aschoff sinuses = mucosal herniations into the muscularis → chronic cholecystitis.
Cholesterolosis = strawberry gallbladder (lipid-laden macrophages).
Porcelain gallbladder & gallstones raise the risk of adenocarcinoma.
GASTROINTESTINAL__Pancreas (exocrine & e:
Overview — One Organ, Two Glands

The pancreas is a mixed gland doing two very different jobs:

🔬 Image slot — pancreas at low power — densely packed serous acini with pale islets of Langerhans scattered among them
Exocrine (~98%)
  • Serous acini making digestive enzymes
  • Drained by a duct system into the duodenum
Endocrine (~1–2%)
  • Islets of Langerhans making hormones
  • Secrete straight into the blood (insulin, glucagon…)
The pale islets scattered among dark serous acini are the instant giveaway that a serous gland is pancreas and not, say, parotid.
How to Recognise It on a Slide ⭐
🔬 Image slot — pancreatic parenchyma — basophilic serous acini, a pale islet, and a centroacinar cell within an acinus
  • Packed serous acini — deeply basophilic cells (RER) with pale, granular apical zones.
  • Pale islets of Langerhans dotted between the acini — the diagnostic feature.
  • Centroacinar cells — pale duct cells sitting inside the acinus (unique to pancreas).
  • No striated ducts and no cartilage — distinguishing it from salivary gland and trachea respectively.
Serous acini + pale islets + centroacinar cells → pancreas. The parotid is also serous but has striated ducts, adipocytes and no islets.
The Exocrine Pancreas — Acini & Zymogens
🔬 Image slot — serous acinar cell — basophilic basal RER and apical eosinophilic zymogen granules
  • Acinar cells are pyramidal: a basophilic base (abundant RER) and apical eosinophilic zymogen granules packed with proenzymes.
  • They secrete a battery of enzymes: proteases (trypsinogen, chymotrypsinogen, proelastase, procarboxypeptidase), amylase, lipase and nucleases.
  • Proteases are released as inactive zymogens and activated only in the duodenum: enterokinase → trypsin, which then activates the rest.
The proteases are secreted as inactive zymogens (amylase, lipase & nucleases leave active); zymogens plus trypsin inhibitors protect against autodigestion. When this fails, enzymes activate within the gland → acute pancreatitis.
The Duct System & Bicarbonate
1
Centroacinar cellsduct cells within the acinus
2
Intercalated → intralobular ducts(no striated ducts)
3
Interlobular → main ductduct of Wirsung → ampulla of Vater
  • Centroacinar and duct cells secrete a watery, bicarbonate-rich alkaline fluid (via CFTR-dependent Cl⁻/HCO₃⁻ exchange) that neutralises gastric acid; loss of CFTR in cystic fibrosis gives thick, HCO₃⁻-poor secretions.
  • Two hormones split the control: secretin → bicarbonate (ductal), CCK → enzymes (acinar); vagal ACh also stimulates.
Secretin = Sodium bicarbonate (ductal); CCK = enzymes (acinar). A reliable way to remember which hormone drives which secretion.
The Endocrine Pancreas — Islets of Langerhans
🔬 Image slot — islet of Langerhans — pale cluster with central beta cells and peripheral alpha cells, surrounded by fenestrated capillaries
  • Beta cells (~70%) — central; secrete insulin (lowers glucose).
  • Alpha cells (~20%) — peripheral; secrete glucagon (raises glucose).
  • Delta cells (~5–10%) — secrete somatostatin (inhibits both).
  • PP (F) cells — pancreatic polypeptide; more common in the head; epsilon cells — ghrelin.
  • Islets are wrapped in a fenestrated capillary network for rapid hormone release.
The tidy β-central / α-peripheral map is the classic rodent pattern; human islets are more intermingled (β ~50–70%). On H&E the cell types look alike (pale) — IHC is needed to tell them apart. Islets are more numerous in the tail. See the Endocrine tab’s Pancreatic Islets of Langerhans note for full detail.
Clinical / Pathological Correlate
Acute pancreatitis
Enzyme autodigestion (gallstones, alcohol) → fat necrosis & saponification; lipase (more specific) & amylase. Complications: pseudocyst (no epithelial lining), necrosis, hypocalcaemia, ARDS; severity by Glasgow/Ranson.
Chronic pancreatitis
Fibrosis, acinar loss & calcification; islets are relatively spared until late → exocrine then endocrine failure
Cystic fibrosis
Inspissated secretions block ducts → acinar atrophy & exocrine insufficiency
Ductal adenocarcinoma
Usually the head; desmoplastic; KRAS/TP53/SMAD4/CDKN2A; precursor PanIN; smoking. Painless jaundice + Courvoisier sign; Trousseau thrombophlebitis; CA19-9 (monitoring); poor prognosis.
Neuroendocrine tumours
Insulinoma (Whipple triad, ↑C-peptide), gastrinoma (ZES; MEN1), glucagonoma (necrolytic migratory erythema), VIPoma (WDHA), somatostatinoma (diabetes/gallstones/steatorrhoea)
Diabetes mellitus
Type 1 = autoimmune β-cell destruction (insulitis); Type 2 = insulin resistance with islet amyloid (IAPP)
⭐ Exam Pearls
Serous acini + pale islets of Langerhans = pancreas.
Centroacinar cells + intercalated ducts, NO striated ducts (vs salivary gland).
Acinar cells: basophilic base (RER) + apical zymogen granules; proteases secreted as inactive zymogens (duodenal enterokinase → trypsin activates the rest; amylase/lipase leave active).
Secretin → bicarbonate (ductal); CCK → enzymes (acinar).
Islet cells: β central (insulin, ~70%), α peripheral (glucagon), δ (somatostatin).
Islets are most numerous in the tail; need IHC to distinguish cell types.
Acute pancreatitis = autodigestion + fat necrosis/saponification; ductal adenocarcinoma = head, desmoplastic, CA19-9, poor prognosis.
Type 1 DM = autoimmune insulitis; Type 2 DM = islet amyloid (IAPP).
GASTROINTESTINAL__Salivary Glands:
Overview — The Saliva Factories

The salivary glands are compound tubuloacinar exocrine glands that make ~1–1.5 L of saliva a day for lubrication, digestion (amylase; lingual lipase from lingual von Ebner glands), protection (lysozyme, lactoferrin, secretory IgA) and buffering.

🔬 Image slot — salivary gland at low power — secretory acini organised into lobules with intercalated and striated ducts between them

There are three paired major glands (parotid, submandibular, sublingual) plus many minor glands. Each is built from two things: secretory units (serous and/or mucous acini) and a branching duct system.

The one feature that pins a serous gland as salivary rather than pancreas is the striated duct — look for it early.
How to Recognise It on a Slide ⭐
🔬 Image slot — salivary parenchyma — dark serous acini, pale mucous acini, a serous demilune, and a striated duct
  • Serous acini — rounded, dark (basophilic) cells with apical granules and a round, basally-placed nucleus.
  • Mucous acini — pale/foamy cells with a flattened basal nucleus.
  • Striated ducts — columnar cells with basal striations (the salivary signature).
  • Myoepithelial (basket) cells around acini and intercalated ducts, and (in mixed glands) serous demilunes capping mucous acini.
Serous ± mucous acini + striated ducts → salivary gland. Then name the gland: all-serous + fat = parotid; mixed serous-dominant + demilunes = submandibular; mostly mucous = sublingual.
The Secretory Cells
Serous cells
  • Rounded, basophilic, apical zymogen granules, round basal nucleus
  • Watery secretion + amylase
Mucous cells
  • Pale, foamy cytoplasm, flattened basal nucleus
  • Viscous mucus secretion
  • Serous demilunes — crescents of serous cells capping mucous acini in mixed glands (often a fixation artefact, but examinable).
  • Myoepithelial (basket) cells — contractile cells (inside the basement membrane) around acini and intercalated ducts that squeeze secretion into the ducts.
Serous = dark & watery (amylase); mucous = pale & sticky. Demilunes are serous crescents; myoepithelial cells do the squeezing.
The Duct System & Why Saliva Is Hypotonic
🔬 Image slot — salivary duct system — intercalated duct, striated duct with basal infoldings and mitochondria, and an excretory duct
1
Intercalated ductlow cuboidal; adds bicarbonate
2
Striated (intralobular) ductcolumnar with basal striations
3
Excretory (interlobular) ductstratified → main duct
  • Striated ducts have basal membrane infoldings packed with mitochondria (the striations) that power ion transport: they reabsorb Na⁺ & Cl⁻ and secrete K⁺/HCO₃⁻.
  • Because they reabsorb more salt than water, the final saliva is hypotonic.
  • Two-stage model: acini make an isotonic, plasma-like primary secretion; the ducts then modify it. At high flow rates there is less time to reabsorb, so saliva becomes less hypotonic (nearer plasma).
Striated ducts are both the identifier of salivary tissue and the reason saliva is hypotonic — two exam points in one structure.
The Three Major Glands
🔬 Image slot — comparison — parotid (pure serous + fat), submandibular (mixed, serous-dominant + demilunes), sublingual (mucous-dominant)
Parotid
Purely serous (amylase-rich), with adipocytes; the facial nerve divides it into superficial/deep lobes (palsy + mass = malignancy); parasympathetic CN IX; Stensen’s duct → opposite the 2nd upper molar
Submandibular
Mixed, serous-predominant with serous demilunes; most resting saliva; parasympathetic CN VII (chorda tympani); Wharton’s duct → floor of mouth (most stones)
Sublingual
Mixed, mucous-predominant; no true capsule; drains via ducts of Rivinus (and Bartholin’s duct)
Parotid = pure serous; submandibular = mixed serous-dominant; sublingual = mucous-dominant. Fat + all-serous acini is the quickest tell for parotid.
Clinical / Pathological Correlate
Sialolithiasis
Duct stones — mostly submandibular (Wharton’s duct); pain/swelling on eating
Mumps parotitis
Paramyxovirus; bilateral parotid swelling; orchitis, oophoritis, pancreatitis, meningitis, deafness; now rare with MMR.
Pleomorphic adenoma
Commonest salivary tumour (benign, parotid); epithelial/myoepithelial cells + myxoid/chondroid stroma; recurs (pseudopodia through the capsule) → superficial parotidectomy; risk of carcinoma ex pleomorphic adenoma.
Warthin’s tumour
Benign, parotid, smokers, older men, often bilateral; oncocytic epithelium + lymphoid stroma; “hot” on technetium scan.
Mucoepidermoid carcinoma
Commonest malignant salivary tumour; mucous + squamous (epidermoid) cells
Adenoid cystic carcinoma
Cribriform (“Swiss-cheese”) pattern; notorious for perineural invasion & pain
Sjögren’s syndrome
Autoimmune lymphocytic sialadenitis → xerostomia + dry eyes (primary or secondary to RA/SLE); anti-Ro/La, Schirmer test, lip-biopsy focus score; MALT lymphoma risk.
Mucocele
Minor-gland duct rupture/blockage (lower lip) → mucus-filled swelling
Acute bacterial sialadenitis
S. aureus ascending the parotid duct in the dehydrated/elderly/post-op (low salivary flow); tender swelling, pus from the duct.
Frey syndrome
Post-parotidectomy gustatory sweating/flushing of the cheek — aberrant regrowth of parasympathetic auriculotemporal fibres onto skin sweat glands.
Rule of 80s: ~80% of salivary tumours are in the parotid, ~80% of those are benign, and ~80% of the benign ones are pleomorphic adenomas. The smaller the gland, the higher the chance a tumour is malignant.
⭐ Exam Pearls
Striated ducts = salivary gland (distinguishes it from pancreas).
Serous = dark, watery, amylase; mucous = pale, sticky; demilunes = serous caps on mucous acini.
Myoepithelial cells squeeze secretion into the ducts.
Striated ducts reabsorb Na⁺/Cl⁻ → saliva is hypotonic.
Parotid = pure serous + fat (Stensen’s, facial nerve); submandibular = mixed serous-dominant (Wharton’s, most stones, most resting saliva); sublingual = mucous-dominant.
Pleomorphic adenoma = commonest (benign, mixed epithelial + chondromyxoid); Warthin’s = smokers/bilateral, oncocytes + lymphoid stroma.
Mucoepidermoid = commonest malignant; adenoid cystic = perineural invasion.
Sjögren’s = xerostomia + dry eyes, anti-Ro/La; rule of 80s for parotid tumours.
